Huygens first systematically studied expected value in his 1692 work *Calculating in Games of Chance*, where he used symmetric gambles to deduce general expected values. His Proposition I was presented as a step in this method and mirrors the approach later popularized by Pascal.

The idea is that in a fair symmetric game where each payoff can occur with the same likelihood, the expectation is simply the arithmetic average of the two possible amounts, reflecting the idea that no outcome is favored.
Huygens’ Proposition I asserts that if a player may receive a payoff of either a or b with equal probability, the expected value of the gamble is (a+b)/2, the half‑sum of a and b.

Huygens proved this by modelling the gamble as a two‑player game in which each player stakes (a+b)/2 and has an equal chance of winning the total stake. The value of the game to each player is then (a+b)/2. Adding a symmetric concession that the winner pays the loser a consolation prize of b does not alter the value by symmetry. In the modified game, if player A wins, he collects the total stake a+b and must pay b to B, leaving him with a; if he loses, he receives b from B. Thus A’s possible outcomes are a or b with equal chance, and the value remains (a+b)/2.
For instance, if a player is offered a game with a 50% chance to win 2 or 8, the expected value is 5, because the game is equivalent to a 5‑5 stake where the loser pays 3—a clearly value‑5 game.
(a+b)/2 is the notation for the expected value in a two‑outcome symmetric gamble, referred to as the half‑sum of the two potential payoffs.

This proposition establishes that for any gamble with two equally likely outcomes a and b, the expected monetary benefit equals the arithmetic mean of a and b, laying the groundwork for the general definition of expected value as a weighted average.

Huygens' Proposition II appears in his 1692 work ‘Calculating in Games of Chance’. It is part of the first systematic study of expected value, extending Pascal’s approach from two outcomes (Prop. I) to three outcomes (Prop. II) and later to an arbitrary number n. The method relies on symmetry arguments and was used by Huygens to formalize expected value before a rigorous probabilistic framework existed.

The intuitive idea is that when each possible result of a gamble is equally likely, a fair game’s value equals the simple average of those results. By arranging a multi‑player stake and distributing consolation prizes, Huygens demonstrates that this average remains unchanged, providing a concrete justification for using the arithmetic mean as the expected value in symmetric situations.
If I expect a, b, or c, either of which, with equal facility, may happen, then the Value of my Expectation is (a + b + c)/3, or the third of the Sum of a, b, and c.

Huygens considered a game among three players A, B, and C, each staking (a + b + c)/3 with an equal chance of winning. The value of the game to player A is the stake. He then modifies the game by adding agreements: if one of the players wins he pays the other a consolation prize of b when B wins, and of c when C wins. These agreements do not change the game's value by symmetry. After the modifications, if A wins the final payoff is a; if B wins, A receives b; if C wins, A receives c. Thus A faces a game where outcomes a, b, c occur with equal probability and has value (a + b + c)/3, proving the proposition.
No explicit numeric example is provided in the text for Proposition II; the proof is presented in general terms for any triple of values a, b, c with equal probability.

a, b, c denote the possible outcomes of the gamble; equal probability is indicated by “with equal facility”; the expected value is expressed as (a + b + c)/3; the stake each player puts in the game is also (a + b + c)/3; consolation prizes of b and c are used in the modified game.

The proposition shows that for a gamble with three equally likely outcomes, the expected value is simply the arithmetic mean of those outcomes. Huygens deduces this by constructing a symmetric multi‑player game and demonstrating that adding consolation payments does not alter the value of a fair game, thereby confirming the averaging rule for equal‑probability cases.

Huygens' third proposition appears in his 1692 work *Calculating in Games of Chance*, where he extends his earlier approach for symmetric outcomes to situations with unequal probabilities. He introduces the idea that if a gambler has two possible winnings, a or b, with different numbers of ways, p and q, of occurring, then the expected value can still be deduced by constructing an equivalent gamble in which each of the p+q equally likely elementary outcomes results in either a or b, respectively. This demonstrates Huygens' method of reducing general problems to symmetric ones before applying the weighted average.

The third proposition is framed as an extension of the first two: Prop. I handled two outcomes with equal probability; Prop. II handled three outcomes with equal probability. Prop. III tackles the two-outcome case with unequal probabilities, a necessary generalization for practical gambling problems where the chances are not symmetric.

The intuition behind Prop. III is that a fair game’s value is proportional to how often each outcome appears; if outcome a occurs p times out of p+q equally likely elementary events and outcome b occurs q times, then the average payoff per event is (p·a + q·b)/(p+q). Thus the expected value is simply the weighted average of the two possible winnings, with weights proportional to the number of favourable elementary events for each outcome.

If a gambler can win a amount with p equally likely chances and a different amount b with q equally likely chances, all elementary events having equal probability, then the value of the expectation is E = (p/(p+q))·a + (q/(p+q))·b.

Huygens constructs a new gamble with p+q elementary outcomes, each equally likely. In p of those outcomes the payoff is a and in the remaining q outcomes the payoff is b. The expected value of this symmetric gamble is the simple arithmetic mean of its p+q outcomes, i.e. (p·a + q·b)/(p+q). By symmetry this value equals the value of the original asymmetric gamble, since the same set of possibilities and same stake can be rearranged without affecting the game’s fairness. Therefore the expected value of the original two‑outcome game with probabilities p/(p+q) and q/(p+q) is precisely (p/(p+q))·a + (q/(p+q))·b.

While the text does not provide an explicit numerical example for Prop. III, the argument applies to any pair of payoffs a and b with rational probabilities p/(p+q) and q/(p+q). For instance, if a gambler could win 6 dollars with 3 out of 4 equally likely elementary events and 10 dollars with 1 out of 4 events (so p=3, q=1), the expected value would be (3/4)·6 + (1/4)·10 = 7.5 dollars.

The proposition uses the symbols p and q to denote the counts of elementary events leading to outcomes a and b, respectively, with p+q total equally likely events. The expected value E is expressed as a weighted sum: E = (p/(p+q))a + (q/(p+q))b.

Prop. III formalizes the idea that expectations for games with unequal outcome probabilities can be determined by treating the probabilities as ratios of equal‑chance elementary events. It shows that the expectation is the weighted average of the outcomes, with weights reflecting the relative frequencies of the events. This reasoning underlies the modern definition of expected value as a sum of outcomes each multiplied by its probability, and illustrates Huygens' early use of combinatorial symmetry to infer general results from particular symmetric cases.

The variance quantifies the average squared deviation from the mean; multiplying a random variable by a constant stretches or compresses its values, so the squared deviations scale by the square of that constant. Because variance is a second‑order moment, it behaves like the square of a standard deviation, hence the factor of $c^2$ when scaling. Adding a constant merely shifts all outcomes and does not change spread, so the variance remains unchanged. When summing independent identically distributed random variables, each contributes additively to the spread, which is reflected by the linear increase of variance with the number of terms. The average reduces spread inversely with the number of observations, leading to a variance that decreases with $1/n$. These patterns illustrate how variance captures dispersion in a way that is sensitive to scaling but insensitive to location changes.

The variance measures how much outcomes of a random experiment tend to deviate from the mean. For independent random variables, fluctuations in one component do not influence another; thus the overall spread of the sum is simply the sum of individual spreads. This additive property distinguishes variance from expectation, which is linear. The result shows that even if individual variables are uncertain, their combined uncertainty grows only linearly with the number of independent terms.

Little's law for queues, 276

Little's law links the three fundamental performance measures of a stable queueing system: arrival rate, average number in the system, and average time a customer spends in the system.  It reflects the idea that, over long periods, the number of customers in the system equals the rate at which customers arrive multiplied by the time they spend in the system.  The law holds even when some customers do not wait at all, as it counts the waiting time of all customers, including those who pass immediately.

The law reflects a conservation principle: over a long period the number of customers entering the system must equal the number leaving. Therefore, the product of how often customers arrive and how long they wait equals the average number that are present. The geometric distribution of queue length shows that higher traffic intensity increases both N and T proportionally, as captured by the formulas.

Little's law for queues states that the expected number of customers in the system, denoted N, equals the product of the arrival rate λ and the expected waiting time T, i.e. N = λ T.  Equivalently, the expected waiting time is given by T = N/λ.

Little's law states that for a stable queuing system the expected number of customers in the system (N) equals the arrival rate (λ) multiplied by the expected waiting time (T), i.e., N=λT. This can be rearranged as T=N/λ. The text presents the specific expression for an M/M/1 queue where the traffic intensity ρ=λ/μ<1: N=ρ/(1-ρ) and T=ρ/(λ(1-ρ))=1/(μ-λ).

Little's law can be derived by an equilibrium argument: when a customer joins the queue he expects to find on average N people ahead of him, and after he leaves he expects to find λ T people behind him.  In equilibrium these two numbers must be equal, yielding N = λ T.  The text indicates that a formal proof is not given here but may be found in Ross; a reference to the literature is provided as footnote 24.

The queue length distribution in equilibrium is geometric with probabilities s_j=(1-ρ)ρ^j for j=0,1,2,… when ρ<1. The expected queue size is the mean of this distribution, N=ρ/(1-ρ). Applying Little's result N=λT gives T=N/λ=ρ/(λ(1-ρ)), which simplifies algebraically to 1/(μ-λ). Thus the expected waiting time in an M/M/1 queue is T=1/(μ-λ).

Example 6.29 applies Little's law to a queue where arrivals occur at rate λ and service times are exponentially distributed with rate μ.  When the traffic intensity ρ = λ/μ is less than 1, the expected queue length N and the expected waiting time T are finite, and Little's law provides the relationship N = λ T.  The example also notes that in simulation (Figure 6.8) the relationship holds, with the queue length distribution estimated by simulation and the waiting times tracked.

Simulation example: arrival rate λ=1 and service rate μ=1.1, giving ρ=1/1.1=10/11. The expected queue size N=ρ/(1-ρ)=10, and the expected waiting time T=1/(μ-λ)=10. The observed simulation averages were 8.19 for queue size and 7.37 for waiting time, close to the theoretical values. The waiting time histogram was exponential with parameter μ-λ, confirming the theoretical distribution.

λ – arrival rate (reciprocal of mean inter‑arrival time); μ – service rate (reciprocal of mean service time); ρ – traffic intensity, defined as λ/μ or equivalently the ratio of average service time to average inter‑arrival time; N – expected number of customers in the queue (queue length); T – expected waiting time of a customer in the queue.  Little's law is expressed as N = λ T, or equivalently T = N/λ.
N – expected number of customers (queue length) in the system; λ – arrival rate; μ – service rate; ρ – traffic intensity defined as λ/μ; T – expected waiting time of a customer.

Little's law provides a fundamental relationship in queuing theory that applies to any stable system irrespective of arrival or service distributions, provided the mean values exist.  It allows one to compute one of the three key metrics (arrival rate, average number in the system, average waiting time) if the other two are known.  The law is particularly useful in designing and evaluating service systems, as it highlights the trade‑off between system capacity, customer arrival intensity, and expected delays.  When the traffic intensity ρ exceeds 1 the queue becomes unstable and the law indicates that either N or T must diverge, whereas for ρ < 1 the law guarantees finite values for both.

Little's law provides a fundamental balance for any stable queue: the average number of customers present equals the average arrival rate times the average time a customer spends in the system. It applies regardless of the underlying distribution of interarrival and service times, provided the system reaches steady state. In the M/M/1 case it yields explicit formulas that link traffic intensity, arrival and service rates to expected queue length and waiting time.

The variance addition formula was introduced within the context of exploring properties of covariance and correlation of random variables in exercise 17 of the text. It formalizes how the variance of a sum depends not only on individual variances but also on their covariance, providing a foundational tool for subsequent discussions of dependence and regression.

The variance addition formula reveals that when two random variables are added, the variability of the resulting sum can be greater, equal to, or smaller than the sum of their individual variances, depending on how they co‑vary. If the variables move in the same direction (positive covariance), the sum is more variable; if they move oppositely (negative covariance), the sum can be less variable. Independence eliminates this extra term, restoring the simple additive property.

For any two random variables (X) and (Y), the variance of their sum is given by (displaystyle V(X+Y)=V(X)+V(Y)+2,operatorname{cov}(X,Y)).  When (X) and (Y) are independent, (operatorname{cov}(X,Y)=0) and the formula reduces to the simpler additive form (V(X+Y)=V(X)+V(Y)).

Exercise 17(c) derives the variance addition formula by expanding the definition of variance (displaystyle V(X+Y)=E[(X+Y)^2]-[E(X+Y)]^2).  After algebraic manipulation this expression becomes (displaystyle V(X)+V(Y)+2,E[(X-mu(X))(Y-mu(Y))]), where the last term is exactly the covariance (operatorname{cov}(X,Y)).  Part (b) of the same exercise shows that if (X) and (Y) are independent, then (operatorname{cov}(X,Y)=0) because (E[(X-mu(X))(Y-mu(Y))]=E[X-mu(X)],E[Y-mu(Y)]=0), yielding the simplified additive result.

1. If (X) and (Y) are independent with (V(X)=4) and (V(Y)=9), then (operatorname{cov}(X,Y)=0) and (V(X+Y)=4+9=13). 
2. If (X) and (Y) have (V(X)=4), (V(Y)=9) and perfect positive correlation (ho=1) (so (operatorname{cov}(X,Y)=sqrt{4cdot9}=6)), then (V(X+Y)=4+9+2cdot6=25=(2+3)^2). 
3. If (X) and (Y) have (V(X)=4), (V(Y)=9) and perfect negative correlation (ho=-1) (so (operatorname{cov}(X,Y)=-6)), then (V(X+Y)=4+9-12=1=(2-3)^2).

(V(X)) denotes the variance of (X).  (operatorname{cov}(X,Y)) denotes the covariance of (X) and (Y), defined as (operatorname{cov}(X,Y)=E igl[(X-mu(X))(Y-mu(Y)) igr]).  The symbol (mu(X)) stands for the expected value (E[X]).

The variance addition formula encapsulates the effect of dependence between variables on the dispersion of their sum.  In statistical modeling, it explains why aggregating correlated measurements can either inflate or deflate overall variability.  It also underpins techniques such as portfolio variance calculation in finance, where the covariance terms represent risk interaction between assets.
For any two random variables X and Y with finite, positive variances, the correlation coefficient defined by ρ(X,Y)=cov(X,Y)/√(V(X)V(Y)) satisfies the inequality -1 ≤ ρ(X,Y) ≤ 1.

From Exercise 17(c) we have V(X+Y)=V(X)+V(Y)+2cov(X,Y).  Let σ(X)=√V(X) and σ(Y)=√V(Y).  Then V(X/σ(X)+Y/σ(Y))=2(1+ρ(X,Y)).  Since variance is non‑negative, 2(1+ρ)≥0, so ρ≥−1.  Similarly, V(X/σ(X)-Y/σ(Y))=2(1−ρ(X,Y))≥0, which forces ρ≤1.  Combining these two inequalities yields −1 ≤ ρ(X,Y) ≤ 1.

The contour or equal‑density ellipse of the bivariate normal distribution has been used in statistical theory since the early 20th century to visualize joint variability, to construct confidence regions, and to study correlation. It is a natural consequence of the Gaussian kernel and has become a standard tool in probability and statistics education.

The quadratic form x^2 - 2ρxy + y^2 captures how the probability mass of a bivariate normal is stretched and tilted in the plane. When ρ = 0 the cross term vanishes and the level curves are circles aligned with the coordinate axes. As ρ moves toward ±1 the ellipse becomes more elongated along the line y = ±x, reflecting stronger positive or negative linear dependence. The parametric equations describe this stretching by scaling the cosθ and sinθ components along orthogonal axes that are aligned with the principal axes of the ellipse.

The set of points (x, y) in the plane where the joint density of a standardized bivariate normal distribution with correlation ρ equals a fixed constant C forms an ellipse whose equation is x^2 - 2ρxy + y^2 = D, where D is a constant that depends on C.

By definition the joint density is f_{X,Y}(x,y) = √{1-ρ^2}^{-1} exp(-(x^2-2ρxy+y^2)/(2(1-ρ^2))), up to a normalizing constant. Setting this equal to a fixed value C and solving for the exponent gives x^2 - 2ρxy + y^2 = -2(1-ρ^2) ln(C·√{1-ρ^2}) = D, which is a quadratic form in (x,y). The quadratic form can be diagonalized by a rotation that removes the cross term, showing that the level set is an ellipse centered at the origin. The eigenvalues of the coefficient matrix are 1-ρ and 1+ρ, which correspond to the squared semi‑axes of the ellipse. The parametric equations x = r cosθ/√{2(1-ρ)} + r sinθ/√{2(1+ρ)} and y = r cosθ/√{2(1-ρ)} - r sinθ/√{2(1+ρ)} arise from substituting the rotation that diagonalizes the quadratic form and scaling by the semi‑axis lengths r/√{2(1-ρ)} and r/√{2(1+ρ)} respectively.

A program can generate 1000 independent pairs (X, Y) from the bivariate normal distribution with ρ = -½, 0, and ½, then overlay the curves defined by the parametric equations for radii r = 1, 2, 3. The resulting plots display concentric ellipses that illustrate how the shape and orientation of the equal‑density contours change as the correlation varies.

ρ denotes the correlation coefficient between the two standardized normal variables; (x, y) are the coordinates in the joint density plot; f_{X,Y}(x,y) is the joint density function; C is a fixed density level; D is the constant that appears on the right‑hand side of the ellipse equation after solving for the exponent; r is a positive scalar controlling the size of the ellipse in the parametric representation; θ is the parametric angle varying from 0 to 2π.

These ellipses represent loci of equal joint probability density; points inside an ellipse have higher probability density than points outside. In practice, they are used to display the dependence structure of two variables, to define confidence ellipses for bivariate mean estimates, and to illustrate how correlation stretches and rotates the region of high probability.

The conditional normal distribution theorem is a foundational result in probability, often illustrated through the study of correlated normal random variables, such as in Galton’s analysis of familial heights. The joint density for a pair of standard normal variables with correlation coefficient ρ was introduced to model such dependence and led to insights on regression toward the mean.

When two standard normal variables X and Y are correlated, knowing a particular value of Y provides information about X. The amount of information is quantified by ρ: a higher |ρ| means a stronger linear relationship and hence a more concentrated conditional distribution of X around a linearly related value. This reflects the idea that observations of one variable constrain the possible values of the other.

For standard normal random variables X and Y with correlation coefficient ρ∈(−1,1), the conditional distribution of X given Y=y is normal with mean μ_{X|Y}(y)=ρ y and variance σ²_{X|Y}=1−ρ². Thus X|Y=y ~ N(ρ y, 1−ρ²).

Given the joint density f_{X,Y}(x,y)=\frac{1}{2π\sqrt{1-ρ^2}}\exp\!Big[-\frac{x^2-2ρxy+y^2}{2(1-ρ^2)}\Big] and the marginal f_Y(y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2π}}\exp(-y^2/2), the conditional density is f_{X|Y}(x|y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}.  Simplifying the exponential exponent yields \!\exp\!Big[-\frac{(x-ρy)^2}{2(1-ρ^2)}\Big], which is the kernel of a normal density with mean ρy and variance 1-ρ^2.  The normalization constant is 1/\sqrt{2π(1-ρ^2)}, confirming that f_{X|Y}(x|y) is a proper normal density.

If ρ=0.5 and Y=1, then X|Y=1 follows N(0.5, 0.75).  The expected value E(X|Y=1)=0.5 is less than the observed y=1, illustrating regression toward the mean.  Similarly, for ρ=−0.4 and Y=−2, E(X|Y=−2)=0.8, closer to 0 than the extreme value – again regression to the mean.

f_{X|Y}(x|y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}.  The joint density for correlated standard normals: f_{X,Y}(x,y)=\frac{1}{2π\sqrt{1-ρ^2}}\exp\!Big[-\frac{x^2-2ρxy+y^2}{2(1-ρ^2)}\Big].  Marginal of Y: f_Y(y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2π}}\exp(-y^2/2).

The theorem quantifies how observing Y updates our belief about X: the conditional mean shifts linearly with y, weighted by ρ, while the conditional variance shrinks by a factor of 1-ρ^2, reflecting increased certainty when variables are strongly correlated.  In practice, this explains phenomena such as taller parents tending to have slightly shorter children on average when both variables are strongly positively correlated – an instance of regression to the mean.

Because convolution sums over all possible pairs (k, j−k) that produce a given sum j, and the choice of which random variable supplies the first component versus the second does not affect the set of pairs, the operation is symmetric.
The convolution operation is commutative, meaning m1 * m2 = m2 * m1 for any two integer‑valued independent random‑variable distributions m1 and m2.
Starting from the definition m3(j)=∑_k m1(k)·m2(j−k), substitute l=j−k. Then m3(j)=∑_l m1(j−l)·m2(l)=∑_l m2(l)·m1(j−l), which is exactly m2 * m1 evaluated at j. Hence m1 * m2 = m2 * m1 for all j.
In Example 7.1, the die distribution m is convolved with itself. Since the same distribution is used, swapping the two factors yields the same result, illustrating commutativity.
The convolution of two integer‑valued random‑variable distributions m1 and m2 is denoted m1 * m2 and defined by m3(j)=∑_k m1(k)·m2(j−k) for all integers j.

Convolution represents the distribution of the sum of two independent random variables. Commutativity means that the distribution of X+Y is the same as that of Y+X, which aligns with the commutative property of addition.

The associative property means that when convolving several independent distributions, the order in which the convolutions are performed does not affect the resulting distribution; grouping the variables in different ways yields the same sum distribution.
The convolution operation on probability mass functions of integer‑valued random variables is associative: for any three such functions m1, m2, and m3, (m1 * m2) * m3 = m1 * (m2 * m3).

It is straightforward to show that the convolution is associative. Since (m1 * m2)(j) = Σk m1(k)m2(j−k), then ((m1 * m2) * m3)(j) = Σℓ (m1 * m2)(ℓ)m3(j−ℓ) = Σℓ Σk m1(k)m2(ℓ−k)m3(j−ℓ). Reindexing the double sum (e.g., let t=ℓ−k) gives the same expression as (m1 * (m2 * m3))(j), proving associativity. This follows from the commutativity and distributivity of summation over integers.

In computing the distribution of S3 = X1+X2+X3, one can first convolve the distributions of X1 and X2 to obtain the distribution of S2, then convolve that result with the distribution of X3; by associativity this is equivalent to first convolving X2 and X3 and then convolving with X1.
m1 * m2 denotes the convolution of distributions m1 and m2.  For integer‑valued random variables, (m1 * m2)(j)=Σk m1(k)m2(j−k).  Associativity is expressed as (m1 * m2) * m3 = m1 * (m2 * m3).

Associativity guarantees that when adding multiple independent discrete random variables, the resulting probability mass function depends only on the individual distributions and not on the sequence in which the variables are combined. This allows recursive computation of sums via successive convolutions and underpins inductive arguments for sums of independent trials.

When two independent random variables X and Y are summed to produce Z = X + Y, the density of Z at a particular point z must account for all pairs (x,y) such that x + y = z. Because X and Y are independent, the joint density of (X,Y) factorizes as f_X(x)f_Y(y). Integrating this product over all y that satisfy x = z – y gives the contribution to f_Z(z). This integral is exactly the convolution of f_X and f_Y, illustrating intuitively how the distribution of the sum is built from the individual distributions.

Let X and Y be independent random variables with density functions f_X(x) and f_Y(y) defined for all real numbers. Then the sum Z = X + Y is a random variable whose density function is given by the convolution of f_X and f_Y: 

f_Z(z) = (f_X * f_Y)(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_X(z - y) f_Y(y) \,dy.

The joint density of (X,Y) is f_X(x)f_Y(y) by independence. The density of the sum Z at z is the probability that X+Y falls in an infinitesimal interval around z, which equals the integral of the joint density over all pairs satisfying x+y=z. Changing variables to y gives

f_Z(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_X(z - y) f_Y(y) \,dy,

which is precisely the definition of the convolution f_X * f_Y. Thus f_Z = f_X * f_Y, establishing the theorem.

Example 7.3 illustrates the theorem for two independent uniform(0,1) variables. Their densities are f_X(x)=f_Y(x)=1 for 0≤x≤1 and 0 otherwise. The convolution integral yields

f_Z(z) = \begin{cases} z,& 0\le z\le 1,\\ 2 - z,& 1<z\le 2,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

This triangular density is the classic distribution of the sum of two dice rolled independently.

Example 7.4 applies the theorem to two independent exponential(λ) variables. Each has density f_X(x)=f_Y(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x} for x≥0. The convolution integral (omitted here for brevity) results in f_Z(z)=\lambda^2 z e^{-\lambda z} for z≥0, the Gamma(2,λ) density.

f_X(x) – density of random variable X.

f_Y(y) – density of random variable Y.

f_Z(z) – density of the sum Z = X + Y.

Convolution of two functions f and g:

(f * g)(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(z - y) g(y) \,dy.

In the theorem, f_X * f_Y denotes the convolution of the two densities.

The theorem formalizes the intuitive idea that the distribution of the sum of independent random variables is obtained by "blending" their individual distributions. Convolution provides a concrete analytic tool: to find the density of a sum, one integrates over all ways the total can be partitioned between the summands. This principle underlies many areas of probability, such as finding distributions of aggregated risks, noise accumulation, or total travel times.

Chebyshev Inequality is introduced as an important inequality needed to discuss the Law of Large Numbers, a fundamental theorem of probability that links the mathematical model to the frequency interpretation of probability.

The text notes that Chebyshev's Inequality is the best possible inequality in the sense that for any ε>0 there exists a discrete random variable for which the inequality holds with equality, illustrating its sharpness.
The inequality is named after P. L. Chebyshev, who first published it in his 1867 paper "On Mean Values" in the Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics (vol. 12, pp. 177–184).
The text cites Chebyshev's original work as a historical reference for the inequality.
The text notes that the theorem (Chebyshev's Inequality) is not necessarily true if the variance \(\sigma^2\) is infinite, referencing Example 8.8.

The bound is named after the Russian mathematician Pafnuty Chebyshev, who first proved it in 1867 as part of his work on the law of large numbers.  It is one of the earliest results linking moments of a distribution to tail probabilities.
Chebyshev Inequality appears in the index of the work, with page references 305 and 316, indicating its inclusion in the literature.
The mathematician Chebyshev, P. L., is cited on page 313 in the same index.

The inequality provides an intuitive bound on how likely a random variable is to deviate far from its mean: the probability of a deviation of at least ε is controlled by the variance of the variable divided by ε², so larger variance or smaller ε leads to larger tail probabilities.
Thus, for a given number of standard deviations k, the chance of exceeding that distance is at most 1/k², showing that extreme deviations become increasingly unlikely.

Chebyshev's Inequality quantifies how unlikely it is for a random variable to deviate far from its mean: the probability of a deviation of at least \(\epsilon\) is at most the variance divided by \(\epsilon^2\).

Because variance measures the average squared distance from the mean, larger variance permits larger deviations, while larger \(\epsilon\) (i.e., more standard deviations) makes the bound smaller, reflecting the intuition that extreme deviations are rare.

Chebyshev's Inequality gives a worst‑case upper bound on the probability that a random quantity deviates from its mean by more than a chosen error \(\epsilon\), based solely on the variance of the underlying distribution.
The bound becomes tighter when the variance is small or when the sample size \(n\) is large, reflecting that averaging reduces variability.

Since variance measures the average squared distance from the mean, the inequality says that only a small fraction of the total squared distance can be contributed by outcomes that lie far away; thus the proportion of outcomes beyond $a$ standard deviations cannot exceed $1/a^2$.
Theorem 8.1 (Chebyshev Inequality): Let X be a discrete random variable with expected value μ=E(X) and let ε>0 be any positive real number. Then P(|X−μ|≥ε)≤V(X)/ε².
Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with density \(f(x)\) having finite expected value \(\mu = E(X)\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2 = V(X)\). For any positive number \(\epsilon > 0\),
\[ P(|X - \mu| \ge \epsilon) \le \frac{\sigma^2}{\epsilon^2}. \]
For a sample mean \(A_n = \frac{S_n}{n}\) of \(n\) independent identically distributed random variables with finite variance \(\sigma^2\), Chebyshev's Inequality states that for any \(\epsilon > 0\)
\[ P\big(|A_n-\mu| \ge \epsilon\big) \le \frac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon^2}. \]
For any random variable $X$ with finite mean $\mu=E[X]$ and finite variance $\sigma^2=Var(X)$, and for any $a>0$, Chebyshev's Inequality states that $P(|X-\mu|\ge a)\le \sigma^2/a^2\,.
Chebyshev Inequality is listed in the index with references to pages 305 and 316.
The proof begins by writing P(|X−μ|≥ε)=∑_{|x−μ|≥ε}m(x), where m(x) is the distribution function of X.
Since V(X)=∑_{x}(x−μ)²m(x), restricting the sum to the set {|x−μ|≥ε} yields a quantity no larger than V(X).
On that restricted set each term (x−μ)² is at least ε², so ∑_{|x−μ|≥ε}(x−μ)²m(x)≥ε²∑_{|x−μ|≥ε}m(x)=ε²P(|X−μ|≥ε).
Combining the inequalities gives ε²P(|X−μ|≥ε)≤V(X), and dividing by ε² yields the desired bound P(|X−μ|≥ε)≤V(X)/ε².

The proof for the continuous case follows exactly the same steps as the discrete case: apply Markov's inequality to the non‑negative random variable \((X-\mu)^2\) to obtain \(P((X-\mu)^2 \ge \epsilon^2) \le E[(X-\mu)^2]/\epsilon^2 = \sigma^2/\epsilon^2\). Since \(|X-\mu| \ge \epsilon\) is equivalent to \((X-\mu)^2 \ge \epsilon^2\), the bound follows. The text states that the proof is omitted because it is analogous to the discrete case.
The proof is omitted in the text; it is said to be identical to the proof in the discrete case.

The inequality follows from Markov's inequality applied to the non‑negative random variable $(X-\mu)^2$.  Markov gives $P((X-\mu)^2\ge a^2)\le E[(X-\mu)^2]/a^2=\sigma^2/a^2$, and the event $(X-\mu)^2\ge a^2$ is equivalent to $|X-\mu|\ge a$.

The inequality yields \[ P\big(|S_n/n| \ge \epsilon\big) \le \frac{1}{n\epsilon^2}. \] A table (Table 8.1) compares these Chebyshev bounds with exact probabilities for \(\epsilon=0.1\), showing the bounds are generally not tight.

Chebyshev's Inequality quantifies how the variance controls the tail behavior of a distribution: the larger the variance, the larger the upper bound on the probability of a large deviation from the mean.
It implies that for any random variable, the chance of deviating more than k standard deviations from the mean is at most 1/k², a universal bound independent of the specific distribution.

The inequality is optimal in the sense that there exist distributions (e.g., a two-point symmetric distribution at ±ε) for which the bound is attained, demonstrating that the result cannot be generally improved.

The inequality provides a universal, distribution‑free upper bound on tail probabilities: regardless of the shape of the distribution, the chance of a large deviation cannot exceed the ratio of variance to the square of the deviation size.

In practical terms, if a random variable has small variance, it is tightly concentrated around its mean, and Chebyshev's bound will be small even for modest \(\epsilon\). Conversely, if variance is large, the bound is weak, reflecting limited information about the distribution's tails.
The result is the key tool for proving weak laws of large numbers, as it shows that averages of independent variables with bounded variance become increasingly concentrated around the common mean.
The inequality guarantees that the probability of a large deviation of the sample mean from the true mean decreases at least as fast as \(1/(n\epsilon^2)\).
Because the bound depends only on variance, it is often conservative; the normal‑case table shows the Chebyshev bound can be far larger than the true probability.
When variance is infinite (e.g., Cauchy distribution), the inequality provides no meaningful bound, and the averaging behavior described by the Law of Large Numbers may break down.

Chebyshev's Inequality provides a universal upper bound on the probability that a random variable deviates from its mean by a specified amount, using only the variance.  It tells us that large deviations are unlikely, regardless of the underlying distribution.
The Law of Large Numbers is sometimes called the law of averages and was historically introduced to connect the mathematical model of probability with the frequency interpretation of probability.
The version stated in the text is often called the "Weak Law of Large Numbers" to distinguish it from the later "Strong Law of Large Numbers" mentioned as an exercise.

Chebyshev introduced the first quantitative form of the law of large numbers in 1867, proving what is now called the weak law using his inequality; this result appears in the text as “Chebyshev, On Mean Values, J. Math. Pure Appl., vol. 12 (1867)”.
The weak law was later refined and distinguished from the strong law, which guarantees almost‑sure convergence; the text contrasts the weak law with the strong law in Exercises 15 and 16.

The weak law asserts that as the number of independent, identically distributed trials grows, the sample average becomes increasingly likely to be close to the true expected value, reflecting the idea that long‑run frequencies converge to theoretical probabilities.

Intuitively, when we repeat a random experiment many times, the empirical average of the outcomes should become close to the theoretical mean; this is the everyday belief that the proportion of heads in many coin tosses will be about one half.
The weak law formalizes this intuition by stating that the probability that the average deviates from the mean by more than any fixed ε becomes arbitrarily small as the number of trials grows.

Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) be an independent trials process with common finite expected value \(\mu = E(X_j)\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2 = V(X_j)\). Define \(S_n = X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n\). Then for any \(\epsilon > 0\), \[P\left(\left|\frac{S_n}{n} - \mu\right| \ge \epsilon\right) \to 0\] as \(n \to \infty\), equivalently \[P\left(\left|\frac{S_n}{n} - \mu\right| < \epsilon\right) \to 1\] as \(n \to \infty\).

For a sequence of independent random variables X₁,…,X_n with common finite mean μ and finite variance σ², the weak law asserts that for every ε>0, \lim_{n\to\infty} P\big(|\tfrac{S_n}{n}-\mu|\ge ε\big)=0, equivalently \lim_{n\to\infty} P\big(|\tfrac{S_n}{n}-\mu|<ε\big)=1, where S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n X_k. (Theorem 8.4)

A more general version allowing non‑identical distributions with uniformly bounded variances (σ_k²<R) is proved in Exercise 12: for any ε>0, \lim_{n\to\infty} P\big(|\tfrac{S_n}{n}-\tfrac{M_n}{n}|<ε\big)=1, where M_n=\sum_{k=1}^n m_k and m_k=E(X_k).

In the concrete coin‑toss setting, letting S_n be the number of heads in n tosses of a fair coin, the weak law gives A_n=S_n/n\to 1/2 in probability; i.e., for any ε>0, P(|A_n-1/2|<ε)\to1 as n\to\infty.

Since the \(X_i\) are independent and identically distributed, \(V(S_n) = n\sigma^2\) and therefore \(V\left(\frac{S_n}{n}\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\). The expected value of the sample average is \(E\left(\frac{S_n}{n}\right) = \mu\). Applying Chebyshev's Inequality, for any \(\epsilon>0\) we have \[P\left(\left|\frac{S_n}{n} - \mu\right| \ge \epsilon\right) \le \frac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon^2}.\] Because the right‑hand side tends to zero as \(n\to\infty\), the probability that the sample average deviates from \(\mu\) by at least \(\epsilon\) also tends to zero, establishing the weak law.

The proof proceeds by applying Chebyshev’s inequality: for each n, P\big(|\tfrac{S_n}{n}-\mu|\ge ε\big)\le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(S_n)}{n^2 ε^2}=\frac{σ^2}{n ε^2}, which tends to 0 as n\to\infty, establishing the weak law for i.i.d. variables. (Theorem 8.4)

For the non‑identical case, Chebyshev gives P\big(|\tfrac{S_n}{n}-\tfrac{M_n}{n}|\ge ε\big)\le \frac{\sum_{k=1}^n\sigma_k^2}{n^2 ε^2}\le \frac{nR}{n^2 ε^2}=\frac{R}{n ε^2}, which again vanishes as n\to\infty, proving the statement in Exercise 12.

In a sequence of Bernoulli trials with success probability \(p\), letting \(X_i = 1\) for a success and \(0\) otherwise gives \(\mu = p\). The weak law states that \(P\bigl(|\frac{S_n}{n} - p| < \epsilon\bigr) \to 1\) as \(n\to\infty\), meaning the proportion of successes converges in probability to \(p\).

For repeated fair coin tosses, \(S_n/n\) is the fraction of heads. The weak law predicts that as the number of tosses grows, the distribution of \(S_n/n\) becomes increasingly concentrated near \(0.5\), and the probability of the fraction lying between .45 and .55 approaches 1.

When rolling a six‑sided die \(n\) times, each roll has expectation \(7/2\). The weak law gives \(P\bigl(|\frac{S_n}{n} - \frac{7}{2}| < \epsilon\bigr) \to 1\) as \(n\to\infty\), so the average roll approaches \(3.5\) with high probability.
Coin‑toss example: a fair coin tossed n times; the weak law predicts that the proportion of heads S_n/n will be within 0.01 of 1/2 with probability exceeding 0.99 for sufficiently large n.

The weak law formalizes the frequency interpretation of probability: the long‑run relative frequency of an event (e.g., heads in coin tossing, successes in Bernoulli trials) converges in probability to the theoretical probability \(p\).
It shows that even when individual outcomes are unpredictable, averaging many independent repetitions yields a quantity that can be predicted with arbitrarily high confidence.

Unlike the strong law, the weak law does not guarantee that the sequence of averages will almost surely settle down to the limit; it only controls the probability of deviation at each finite stage.
In practical terms, the weak law justifies using the empirical average as an estimator of the mean when the sample size is large, because the estimator is highly likely to be close to the true value.

By replacing factorials in the binomial distribution with this approximation, he obtained a Gaussian‐type expression for the probability distribution of the sum of many Bernoulli trials.

Theorem 9.1 is derived from Stirling's approximation applied to the factorials in the binomial probability mass function, yielding a normal‐distribution–type form for large sample sizes.

The binomial distribution for large (n) behaves like a normal distribution because the sum of many independent Bernoulli trials concentrates around its mean and the shape of the probability mass function smooths out into a bell‑shaped curve.

Let (b(n,p,j)= inom{n}{j}p^jq^{,n-j}) be the probability that a binomial random variable equals (j). Define (x=(j-np)/sqrt{npq}). Then for large (n), the product (sqrt{npq},b(n,p,j)) is approximately equal to (phi(x)=(1/sqrt{2pi})e^{-x^{2}/2}); equivalently (b(n,p,j)approx phi(x)/sqrt{npq}).

Lindeberg found a condition on the sequence ${X_n}$ that guarantees that the distribution of the sum $S_n$ is asymptotically normally distributed.
Feller showed that Lindeberg’s condition is necessary as well, in the sense that if the condition does not hold then the sum $S_n$ is not asymptotically normally distributed.
The precise statement of Lindeberg’s theorem is found in Feller’s *Introduction to Probability Theory and its Applications*, vol. 1, 3rd ed., p. 254.
Lindeberg’s contribution relaxed the identical–distribution requirement of the classical central limit theorem by providing a more general sufficient condition for asymptotic normality.

Lindeberg’s condition imposes a restriction on the contribution of large individual summands to the total variance; it requires that no single or small group of summands dominates the variance as the number of terms grows.

Intuitively, if each term’s variance contributes only a small portion of the total variance, then the collective effect of many small, independent terms will approximate a normal distribution, regardless of the individual terms’ distributions.

Lindeberg’s theorem states that for a sequence of independent random variables ${X_n}$ with finite variances, if Lindeberg’s condition holds, then the standardized sum $S_n^*= rac{S_n-sum_{i=1}^nmu_i}{sqrt{sum_{i=1}^nsigma_i^2}}$ converges in distribution to a standard normal random variable as $n	oinfty$.

The condition requires that for every $varepsilon>0$ the sum of the variances of those $X_i$ whose absolute deviation from their mean exceeds $varepsilon$ times the total standard deviation tends to zero as $n$ increases.

The text does not provide a full proof of Lindeberg’s theorem; it merely references Feller for the precise statement and proof. The proof involves verifying that Lindeberg’s condition ensures the Lindeberg–Feller central limit theorem applies, which establishes convergence of the characteristic functions to that of the normal distribution.

The moment generating function g(t)=E(e^{tX}) expands into a power series whose coefficients are the moments μ_k=E(X^k). Thus g(t) encodes all moments of X. For a discrete random variable with a finite range, the set of all moments uniquely determines the probability mass function, because each mass point contributes a distinct exponential term e^{t x_j} with coefficient p(x_j). Consequently, if two such distributions have the same mgf, they must assign the same probabilities to the same mass points.

Theorem 10.1: Let X be a discrete random variable with finite range {x_1,x_2,…,x_n} and distribution function p. Its moment generating function g(t)=∑_{j=1}^{n} e^{t x_j}p(x_j) is uniquely determined by p, and conversely, knowing g(t) uniquely determines the set {x_j} and the probabilities {p(x_j)}.

1. p determines g: substituting the definition of p into g(t) gives g(t)=∑_{j=1}^{n} e^{t x_j}p(x_j). 2. Conversely, assume g(t) is known. Because p(x_j)>0 for all j and x_1<⋯<x_n, the function g(t) can be written as a finite sum of distinct exponential terms. By analyzing the exponential terms of g(t) (e.g., through its derivatives at t=0 or via analytic continuation), one can recover each exponent x_j and its coefficient p(x_j). Thus g(t) determines the values of the mass points and their probabilities. Hence g is a one‑to‑one mapping between the distribution p and the mgf.

Example 10.1: For a uniform distribution on {1,…,n}, the mgf is g(t)=n^{-1}(e^t+e^{2t}+⋯+e^{nt}).  The form of g(t) shows that the masses are equal and located at the integers 1,…,n, matching the distribution.  Example 10.2: For a binomial distribution with parameters n and p, g(t)=(pe^t+q)^n.  The binomial form of g(t) uniquely identifies the distribution.  Example 10.3: For a geometric distribution on {1,2,…} with success probability p, g(t)=pe^t/(1−qe^t).  This rational function characterizes the geometric distribution uniquely.  Example 10.4: For a Poisson distribution with mean λ, g(t)=e^{λ(e^t−1)}.  The exponential form of g(t) uniquely determines the Poisson law.
μ_k=E(X^k)=∑_{j} x_j^k p(x_j)

The theorem confirms that in the discrete finite‑range case the mgf is a complete invariant of the distribution: two distributions have identical mgf iff they are identical.  It provides a practical method for determining a distribution from its mgf and underpins the solution of the moment problem in this setting.

The relationship $g_{Z}(t)=g_{X}(t)g_{Y}(t)$ for independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ was observed in Chapter 7 as a consequence of the convolution formula for the distribution of $Z=X+Y$, and later re‑derived using moment‑generating functions in the generating‑function framework of this chapter.

Because $e^{tX}$ and $e^{tY}$ are independent when $X$ and $Y$ are independent, the expectation of their product factorises, so the MGF of the sum naturally becomes the product of the individual MGFs. This mirrors the fact that convolution in the probability domain corresponds to multiplication in the transform domain.

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables with moment‑generating functions $g_{X}(t)=E(e^{tX})$ and $g_{Y}(t)=E(e^{tY})$, then the moment‑generating function of their sum $Z=X+Y$ is 
$$g_{Z}(t)=E(e^{tZ})=E(e^{t(X+Y)})=g_{X}(t),g_{Y}(t).$$

Since independence of $X$ and $Y$ implies independence of the functions $e^{tX}$ and $e^{tY}$, we have 
$$E(e^{tX}e^{tY})=E(e^{tX})E(e^{tY}).$$
Replacing the left‑hand side by $E(e^{t(X+Y)})$ yields 
$$g_{Z}(t)=E(e^{tZ})=g_{X}(t)g_{Y}(t).$$

Example 10.5: For independent binomial variables $X$ and $Y$ with $p_X(j)=p_Y(j)=\binom{n}{j}p^{j}q^{n-j}$, the MGFs are $g_X(t)=g_Y(t)=(pe^{t}+q)^{n}$. Their sum $Z=X+Y$ has MGF $g_Z(t)=(pe^{t}+q)^{2n}$, which corresponds to a binomial distribution with parameters $2n$ and $p$.

Example 10.6: For independent geometric variables $X$ and $Y$ with $p_X(j)=p_Y(j)=q^{j}p$, the MGFs are $g_X(t)=g_Y(t)=\frac{p}{1-qe^{t}}$. The sum $Z=X+Y$ has MGF $g_Z(t)=\frac{p^{2}}{1-2qe^{t}+q^{2}e^{2t}}$, which is the MGF of a negative‑binomial distribution.

$g_Y(t)$ and $g_Z(t)$ are defined analogously for $Y$ and $Z=X+Y$.

The product formula $g_{X+Y}(t)=g_X(t)g_Y(t)$ encapsulates the convolution of the probability mass functions $p_X$ and $p_Y$ into a simple algebraic multiplication. Consequently, the coefficients of the power‑series expansion of $g_{X+Y}(t)$ (or of the ordinary generating function $h_{X+Y}(z)$) directly yield the probability distribution of the sum.

Adding two independent binomial random variables with the same success probability p corresponds to performing twice as many independent Bernoulli trials; the total number of successes is therefore distributed as a binomial with parameters equal to the sum of the numbers of trials and the common probability p.

If X and Y are independent binomial random variables with parameters X∼Bin(n,p) and Y∼Bin(n,p), then the sum Z=X+Y has a binomial distribution Bin(2n,p), i.e. p_Z(j)=∈_{j=0}^{2n} inom{2n}{j}p^jq^{2n-j}. More generally, if X∼Bin(n_1,p) and Y∼Bin(n_2,p) are independent, then Z∼Bin(n_1+n_2,p).

The moment generating functions of X and Y are g_X(t)=(p,e^t+q)^n and g_Y(t)=(p,e^t+q)^n, where q=1-p. Independence implies g_Z(t)=g_X(t)g_Y(t)=(p,e^t+q)^{2n}. This is the moment generating function of a Bin(2n,p) random variable, since the general form of the mgf of Bin(m,p) is (p,e^t+q)^m. Consequently, the probability mass function of Z is p_Z(j)= rac{1}{j!}h_Z^{(j)}(0)= inom{2n}{j}p^jq^{2n-j}, obtained by expanding (p,z+q)^{2n} as an ordinary generating function. The same conclusion follows by noting that the ordinary generating functions satisfy h_Z(z)=h_X(z)h_Y(z)=(p,z+q)^{2n}.

The text presents Example 10.6 in which two independent geometric random variables with common success probability p are summed and the resulting distribution is identified as a negative binomial distribution. This example is the first explicit demonstration of the general principle that the sum of independent geometric distributions yields a negative binomial distribution. The derivation uses generating functions and shows how the resulting probability mass function matches the standard form of a negative binomial with shape parameter r=2.

A geometric random variable counts the number of failures before the first success in a sequence of Bernoulli trials. Summing two such independent counts is equivalent to counting failures before the second success in a sequence of trials, which is exactly what a negative binomial distribution models. The generating‑function calculation confirms this intuition by producing a coefficient that grows linearly with j, the familiar {j+1} factor of a NB(2,p) distribution.

Theorem 10.2 is built upon earlier work on extinction probabilities for branching processes, notably Reverend H. W. Watson’s first incorrect solution, which mistakenly claimed that extinction occurs with probability 1 in all cases due to a miscalculation.

Earlier communication by Bienaymé (1845) anticipated Galton and Watson by 28 years and correctly identified that the extinction probability depends on the mean offspring number, though his detailed reasoning was never fully published.

The text cites Heyde and Seneta’s translation of Bienaymé’s work, noting that when the mean offspring ratio equals or exceeds unity, families may survive with a probability less than one, providing the foundation for the correct solution that Theorem 10.2 presents.

The recursive characterization of generating functions in branching processes originates from the classical work on Galton–Watson processes and is a standard tool in modern probability theory. The text references the use of these recursions to compute extinction probabilities and moments, a technique dating back to the early 20th‑century study of population dynamics.

The recursion $h_{n+1}=h_ncirc h$ expresses the idea that the $n+1$‑st generation is obtained by applying the same offspring distribution to every individual of the $n$‑th generation; thus the generating function of the next generation is the composition of the current generating function with the single‑generation generating function. The extinction recursion $d_n=h(d_{n-1})$ captures the probability that the process dies out by generation $n$ as the probability that a single individual has zero children in a process whose “effective” extinction probability at the previous generation is $d_{n-1}$.
For a branching process with offspring generating function $h(z)$, the generating function $h_n(z)$ of the population size in generation $n$ satisfies the recursive equation $h_{n+1}(z)=h_n(h(z))$.
The extinction probability up to generation $n$ follows the recursion $d_n = h(d_{n-1})$ with initial value $d_1=p_0$.

Starting from $h_{n+1}(z)=E(z^{Z_{n+1}})=sum_kE(z^{Z_{n+1}}mid Z_n=k)P(Z_n=k)$ and noting that when $Z_n=k$, $Z_{n+1}=X_1+cdots+X_k$ where the $X_i$ are i.i.d. with generating function $h(z)$, we have $E(z^{Z_{n+1}}mid Z_n=k)=(h(z))^k$. Substituting into the sum gives $h_{n+1}(z)=sum_k(h(z))^kP(Z_n=k)=h_n(h(z))$. Differentiating the identity with respect to $z$ and using the chain rule yields $h'_{n+1}(z)=h'_n(h(z))h'(z)$. Evaluating at $z=1$ and using $h(1)=1$, $h'(1)=m$ and $h'_n(1)=m_n$, we obtain $m_{n+1}=m_nm$, which inductively gives $m_n=m^n$. The recursion $d_n=h(d_{n-1})$ follows from the definition $d_n=P(Z_n=0)$ and the same conditioning argument applied to extinction events.

The exponential growth property of the mean number of offspring in a branching process is derived from the classical work of Galton and Watson on extinction probabilities, where the generating function technique was introduced to study the evolution of the process across generations.

The analysis presented here follows the exposition in the cited text, where the generating function of the offspring distribution, $h(z)$, and its derivative at 1, $h'(1)$, are used to obtain the recursive mean formula $m_{n+1}=m_n,m$, leading to $m_n=m^n$ for supercritical processes.

The mean number of individuals in generation $n$ is simply the expected number of children produced by each individual in generation $n-1$ multiplied by the expected number in that previous generation.  If each individual, on average, produces more than one child ($m>1$), then each successive generation, on average, will contain more individuals than the one before, and the increase follows a multiplicative pattern.  This multiplicative pattern naturally results in an exponential increase in the average size of the population over time.

Let $m$ denote the expected number of offspring produced by a single parent, that is $m=h'(1)=p_1+2p_2+3p_3+cdots$ for a discrete offspring distribution.  If $m>1$ the branching process is supercritical and the mean number of individuals in the $n$‑th generation, $m_n$, satisfies the recurrence $m_{n+1}=m_ncdot m$.  Solving this recurrence yields $m_n=m^n$, so the mean grows exponentially at rate $m$ as $n	oinfty$.

Starting from the generating function of the population size $h_{n}(z)$, differentiation gives $h_{n+1}'(z)=h'_n(h(z)),h'(z)$.  Setting $z=1$ and using $h(1)=1$, $h'(1)=m$, and $h_n'(1)=m_n$, we obtain $m_{n+1}=m_ncdot m$.  Repeatedly applying this identity gives $m_n=m^n$, since $m_1=m$.  When $m>1$, each multiplication by $m$ increases the mean, producing exponential growth.

In the branching process of Example 10.8, the offspring probabilities are $p_0=0.2$, $p_1=0.5$, $p_2=0.3$, giving $m=p_1+2p_2=1.1>1$.  Consequently, the expected number of individuals in generation $n$ is $1.1^n$, confirming the exponential growth property for this specific case.  For a geometric offspring distribution with parameters $b$ and $c$ in Example 10.11, the mean is $m= rac{b}{(1-c)^2}$; when $m>1$ the same $m_n=m^n$ relationship holds.

$m$ – mean (expected) number of offspring produced by a single parent; $m_n$ – mean number of individuals in the $n$‑th generation; $h(z)$ – probability generating function of the offspring distribution; $h'(1)$ – derivative of $h$ at $z=1$, equal to $m$; $h_n(z)$ – generating function of the population size in generation $n$.

The normalized population size $W_n=Z_n/m^n$ in a Galton–Watson branching process converges in distribution as $n	oinfty$ to a non–degenerate random variable $W$ when the mean offspring number $m>1$ and the extinction probability $d<1$; when $m=1$ the process is critical and $W_n$ converges to zero a.s.; and when $m<1$ the process becomes extinct a.s. with probability one.

For the subcritical case $m<1$ the probabilities of having a specific scaled number of individuals satisfy $m^nP(Z_n=[tm^n])	o(1-d)^2e^{-t(1-d)}$ for every $t>0$, and the extinction probability satisfies $P(Z_n=0)	o d$ as $n	oinfty$.

More generally, for a broad class of branching processes, under suitable regularity conditions there exists a deterministic function $k(t)$ such that $m^nP(Z_n=[tm^n])	o k(t)$ for $t>0$ and $P(Z_n=0)	o d$ as $n	oinfty$.

The theorem provides an asymptotic approximation for the probability that a sum of independent, identically distributed integer‑valued random variables equals a particular integer value. In the context of branching processes, its form is used for comparison with the limiting probabilities of the population size, showing a structural similarity between the two limiting behaviours.

The main difficulty in proving a CLT for discrete integer‑valued random variables is that the distribution functions p_n^*(x) are only defined at points j/√n, so they do not form a simple function over ℝ.  By extending each discrete distribution to a step function τ̅p(x) (equal to p(j) on the interval (j‑½, j+½)) we obtain a genuine density function on ℝ and can then apply Fourier‑analytic techniques.  The extra sinh factor in the modified moment generating function τ̅g_n^*(t) tends to 1, so the limit behaviour is the same as in the continuous case, yielding convergence to the normal density.

For a bounded discrete random variable X taking integer values, with mean μ = 0 and variance σ² = 1, and for independent trials X₁, X₂, …, Xₙ having density p(j), let Sₙ = ∑_{i=1}^n Xᵢ and Sₙ^* = Sₙ/√n.  Define the step‑function extension of the distribution by τ̅p(x)=p(j) for j−½ ≤ x < j+½ and zero otherwise.  Then the step‑function densities τ̅p_n^*(x) of the standardized sums converge pointwise to the standard normal density 1/√(2π) e^{−x²/2} as n→∞.  Consequently the distribution functions F_n^*(a)=P(S_n^*≤a) converge to Φ(a)=∫_{−∞}^a 1/√(2π) e^{−x²/2}dx.  The theorem holds under the stated hypotheses, and the greatest common divisor condition on the support of X is not required in the sketch provided.

Define τ̅p(x) as the step function that equals p(j) on (j−½, j+½).  Its moment generating function is τ̅g(t)=∫_{−∞}^∞ e^{tx}τ̅p(x)dx=g(t)sinh(t/2)/(t/2), where g(t)=∑_{j}p(j)e^{tj}.  Similarly, τ̅g_n(t)=g_n(t)sinh(t/2)/(t/2) and τ̅g_n^*(t)=g_n^*(t)sinh(t/(2√n))/(t/(2√n)).  Since g_n^*(t)→e^{t²/2} as n→∞ and sinh(t/(2√n))/(t/(2√n))→1 by L’Hôpital’s rule, we conclude τ̅g_n^*(t)→e^{t²/2}.  By the Fourier inversion theorem for characteristic functions, this convergence of moment generating functions implies that τ̅p_n^*(x)→(1/√(2π))e^{−x²/2} for all x, establishing the limit distribution.  The step function extension allows the use of continuous‑analysis tools even though the original distributions are purely discrete.

Theorem 9.3 demonstrates that even for integer‑valued bounded random variables, the properly normalized sum behaves asymptotically like a continuous normal variable.  The step‑function extension provides a bridge between discrete probability masses and continuous density functions, enabling the application of characteristic‑function arguments.  The theorem’s conclusion—that the distribution functions converge to the standard normal distribution and that the densities converge to the Gaussian density—confirms the universality of the normal law in the CLT setting.

The extinction probability of a branching process, denoted by $d$, has been studied in the context of modeling chain letter schemes, where each participant may pass the letter to a random number of new participants. In the examined example (Example 10.14), the process was simulated for twelve generations using two different offspring distributions: a finite distribution with $p_0=0.2$, $p_1=0.5$, and $p_2=0.3$, and a Poisson distribution with mean $m=1.1$. For the finite case, a computational program (Branch) estimated the probability that the process dies out by the twelfth generation to be $d_{12}=0.599$, which matched the empirical result of 12 out of 20 simulated runs going extinct by generation twelve. For the Poisson case, the same program produced a survival probability $1-d_{12}=0.232$, so that $d_{12}=0.768$; this theoretical value agreed with the observation that only 6 out of 20 simulated runs yielded a profit, implying survival beyond generation twelve. These simulations provide practical evidence of how extinction probabilities behave in finite time horizons.

The extinction probability is the chance that a branching process eventually reaches a state with no individuals. In a branching process where each individual produces on average $m$ offspring, if $m>1$ the process is supercritical and has a non‑zero chance of surviving indefinitely, whereas if $mle1$ it will almost surely die out. The example illustrates that even when $m$ is slightly greater than one ($m=1.1$), extinction by a fixed generation can still be quite likely: $d_{12}=0.599$ for a bounded offspring distribution and $d_{12}=0.768$ for a Poisson distribution. This demonstrates that the probability of extinction by a finite generation can remain substantial even in a supercritical process.

For a branching process with offspring distribution ${p_j}_{jge0}$ and generating function $f(z)=sum_{j=0}^infty p_j z^j$, the extinction probability $d$ is the smallest non‑negative solution of $d=f(d)$. When the process is observed only up to generation $n$, the probability that it dies out by generation $n$ is denoted $d_n$, which can be computed iteratively using $d_{k+1}=f(d_k)$ with $d_0=0$. In the chain‑letter example, $d_{12}$ was computed using a program and found to be $0.599$ for the finite distribution case and $0.768$ for the Poisson case. The probability of receiving a bonus at or after the twelfth generation is thus $1-d_{12}$, equal to $0.401$ in the finite case and $0.232$ in the Poisson case.

The extinction probability at generation $n$ follows from the recursive relation $d_{k+1}=f(d_k)$, where $f$ is the offspring generating function. Starting from $d_0=0$, repeated application yields $d_{12}$. For the finite distribution with $p_0=0.2$, $p_1=0.5$, $p_2=0.3$, the generating function is $f(z)=0.2+0.5z+0.3z^2$. Iterating this function twelve times gives $d_{12}approx0.599$, matching the simulation result where 12 out of 20 runs died by generation twelve. In the Poisson case with mean $m=1.1$, the generating function is $f(z)=e^{1.1(z-1)}$. Iterating $f$ twelve times yields $d_{12}approx0.768$, implying a survival probability of $0.232$, which accords with the observation that 6 out of 20 simulated runs yielded a profit. These calculations confirm the theoretical extinction probabilities for the specified distributions.

Example 1: Finite distribution with $p_0=0.2$, $p_1=0.5$, $p_2=0.3$ and mean $m=1.1$. The extinction probability by the twelfth generation is $d_{12}=0.599$; consequently the probability of at least one payment from the twelfth generation (i.e., survival beyond that generation) is $1-d_{12}=0.401$. In simulation, 12 of 20 trials died by generation twelve, closely matching the theoretical $d_{12}$. Example 2: Poisson distribution with mean $m=1.1$. The generating function is $f(z)=e^{1.1(z-1)}$. Iterating this function twelve times yields $d_{12}=0.768$, so the survival probability at generation twelve is $1-d_{12}=0.232$. Simulation of 20 trials produced profit in only 6 runs, consistent with the theoretical survival probability. Example 3: In the chain‑letter problem with $p_0>1/2$, the process is subcritical and the extinction probability is $1$, meaning one cannot expect a profit. This is a direct consequence of the general property that if $p_0>1/2$, then $mle1$ and extinction occurs almost surely.

$d_n$ denotes the probability that a branching process has died out by generation $n$; $d$ is the limiting extinction probability as $n	oinfty$. The offspring generating function $f(z)=sum_{j=0}^infty p_j z^j$ encodes the distribution ${p_j}$ of the number of offspring per individual. In the Poisson case the generating function simplifies to $f(z)=e^{m(z-1)}$, where $m$ is the mean number of offspring. The survival probability at generation $n$ is given by $1-d_n$.

The computed values of $d_{12}$ illustrate that even in a supercritical branching process (where each individual on average produces more than one offspring), the probability that the process will have gone extinct by a finite time can be large. For the chain‑letter model with modest over‑one mean, approximately two‑thirds of the processes will have died out by generation twelve. The difference between the finite and Poisson models reflects how the tail of the offspring distribution affects extinction: the Poisson distribution allows for larger numbers of offspring with small probability, slightly reducing extinction probability by generation twelve compared to the bounded case. These extinction probabilities directly determine expected gains: a higher chance of survival translates into a higher chance of receiving bonuses from later generations.

The composition property of probability generating functions, such as h(z)=g(f(z)) for a random sum S_N, is a classical result in the theory of branching processes and compound distributions, dating back to early 20th‑century work on Galton‑Watson processes.

The generating function for the Poisson distribution, h(z)=e^{m(z-1)}, was first derived by Siméon‑Denis Poisson and later popularized in probability textbooks as a canonical example of an infinitely divisible law.

If each summand X_i contributes a factor f(z)=E(z^{X_i}) to the overall generating function, then conditioning on the random count N simply raises this factor to the N‑th power; averaging over N replaces the power by the generating function g of N, yielding the composition g∘f.
In a branching process, one generation’s offspring distribution is described by f(z); applying f again corresponds to two generations, which is why the two‑step generating function is f(f(z)).

For independent integer‑valued random variables X_1,X_2,… with common probability generating function f(z) and an independent integer‑valued random variable N with probability generating function g(z), the probability generating function of the random sum S_N= X_1+…+X_N (with the convention S_0=0) is h(z)=g(f(z)).

Starting from the definition h(z)=E(z^{S_N}), condition on the value of N: h(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}E(z^{S_N}\mid N=k)P(N=k). Since the X_i are independent and identically distributed, E(z^{S_N}\mid N=k)=\big(E(z^{X_1})\big)^k = f(z)^k. Hence h(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}f(z)^k P(N=k)=g(f(z)), which is exactly the composition of the two generating functions.

If each X_i is Poisson with mean m, then f(z)=e^{m(z-1)}. For a Poisson‑distributed N with mean \lambda, g(z)=e^{\lambda(z-1)} and the random sum S_N has generating function h(z)=e^{\lambda(e^{m(z-1)}-1)}.

In the chain‑letter branching model, the offspring distribution of a single parent has generating function f(z). After two generations the total number of descendants has generating function f(f(z)), illustrating the same composition principle for the special case where N itself follows the distribution described by f.
S_N = \sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i \;\text{(random sum)}
X_i \;\text{independent, identically distributed integer‑valued random variables}
N \;\text{independent integer‑valued random variable}
f(z)=E(z^{X_1}) \;\text{probability generating function of each X_i}
g(z)=E(z^{N}) \;\text{probability generating function of N}

The composition h(z)=g(f(z)) provides a compact way to derive the full distribution of a random sum without enumerating all possible combinations of N and the X_i’s. By differentiating h(z) at z=1 one obtains moments of S_N, such as its mean E[S_N]=g'(1)\,E[X_1] and variance Var(S_N)=g''(1)E[X_1]^2+g'(1)Var(X_1).

In branching processes, the same principle explains why the generating function after k generations is the k‑fold self‑composition f^{\circ k}(z), reflecting the iterative nature of offspring production.
The use of generating functions to study branching processes was pioneered by Galton and Watson in the 19th century.
Composing the generating function with itself reflects the two successive independent stages of reproduction in a branching process.
If f(z) is the generating function of the number of offspring produced by a single parent, then the generating function for the total number of offspring after two generations is h(z)=f(f(z)).

Let Z1 be the number of offspring of the initial individual, with generating function f(z). For each of these Z1 individuals, let Zi (i=2,…,Z1+1) be the number of their offspring. The total number after two generations is S=∑_{i=2}^{Z1+1} Zi. Conditionally on Z1=k, the generating function of S is [f(z)]^k, because the Zi’s are i.i.d. with generating function f(z). Taking expectation over Z1 gives E[z^S] = ∑_{k} f(z)^k P(Z1=k) = f(f(z)).
If the offspring distribution is finite with probabilities p0, p1, p2, then f(z)=p0+p1 z+p2 z^2 and h(z)=f(f(z))=p0+p1(p0+p1 z+p2 z^2)+p2(p0+p1 z+p2 z^2)^2.
For a Poisson( m ) distribution, f(z)=exp(m(z−1)). Hence h(z)=f(f(z))=exp(m(exp(m(z−1))−1)).
f(z) = Σ_{j≥0} p_j z^j, the generating function of the offspring distribution.
h(z) = f(f(z)), the generating function after two generations.
The coefficient of z^n in h(z) gives the probability that exactly n individuals are produced after two generations.

Theorem 10.3 shows that if a continuous random variable X has bounded support—specifically, its range lies in the finite interval [−M,M]—then its moment generating function (MGF) g(t)=∑ₖ≥0 μₖtᵏ/k! converges for every real value of t.  Because the support is bounded, the k‑th moment μₖ is dominated by Mᵏ, which guarantees that the power series has an infinite radius of convergence.  Consequently g(t) defines a smooth, infinitely differentiable function on the entire real line, and the nth derivative of g evaluated at 0 reproduces the nth moment μₙ.  This is the continuous analogue of the fact that a discrete MGF always converges for all t; Theorem 10.3 guarantees the same property for continuous variables with bounded support.

Let X be a continuous random variable whose range is contained in the interval [−M,M].  For each integer k≥0, define the k-th moment μₖ=∫_{−M}^{M}xᵏf_X(x)dx, where f_X is the density of X.  Then the power series g(t)=∑_{k=0}^{∞} μₖ tᵏ/k! converges for every real t, defines an infinitely differentiable function g(t), and for each n≥0 we have g^{(n)}(0)=μₙ.

The proof proceeds by bounding each moment μₖ.  First, by definition, |μₖ|≤∫_{−M}^{M}|x|ᵏf_X(x)dx.  Because |x|≤M on the support, we obtain |μₖ|≤Mᵏ∫_{−M}^{M}f_X(x)dx=Mᵏ, since the integral of the density over its support equals 1.  Thus the coefficients of the power series satisfy |μₖ|/k!≤Mᵏ/k!.  The ratio test (or comparison with the exponential series) shows that the series ∑_{k}Mᵏ|t|ᵏ/k! converges for all t, implying that the original series converges for all t.  Because the series converges uniformly on every bounded interval, termwise differentiation is valid; each term μₖtᵏ/k! differentiates to μₖt^{k−1}/(k−1)!, yielding g^{(n)}(t)=∑_{k=n}^{∞} μₖ t^{k−n}/(k−n)!.  Evaluating at t=0 collapses all terms except the one with k=n, giving g^{(n)}(0)=μₙ.  Hence g(t) is infinitely differentiable and its derivatives at zero equal the moments of X.

Example 10.15: X is uniformly distributed on [0,1] (so M=1).  Its moments are μₙ=1/(n+1), and the MGF is g(t)=(e^t−1)/t, which converges for all real t.  This concrete case illustrates Theorem 10.3: the support is bounded, the series converges everywhere, and differentiating g(t) at 0 reproduces the moments.

Example 10.16 and 10.17 (exponential and normal distributions) illustrate that when the support is unbounded, the series may fail to converge for all t.  Thus Theorem 10.3 highlights the special status of bounded random variables.

X – continuous random variable with density f_X(x);  μₖ – the k‑th moment, μₖ=E[X^k] = ∫ x^k f_X(x) dx;  g(t) – moment generating function defined by the power series g(t)=∑_{k≥0} μₖ t^k/k!;  M – non‑negative bound such that the support of X lies in [−M,M];  f_X(x) – density function of X.
The uniqueness of a distribution from its characteristic function is a classical result in probability theory; Theorem 10.4 applies this to the mgf of bounded variables.

The mgf contains all moments of X, and for bounded variables these moments are finite and sufficient to reconstruct the characteristic function; via Fourier inversion this characteristic function yields the density, guaranteeing uniqueness.
Theorem 10.4 states that if X is a bounded random variable, then the moment generating function g_X(t) of X determines the density function f_X(x) uniquely.
The mgf of X is defined by the series g_X(t)=∑_{k=0}^∞ μ_k t^k/k! and equivalently by the integral g_X(t)=∫_{-∞}^{∞} e^{tx} f_X(x) dx.
Replacing t by iτ with τ∈ℝ gives the series g_X(iτ)=∑_{k=0}^∞ μ_k (iτ)^k/k! which converges for all τ, allowing us to define the characteristic function k_X(τ)=g_X(iτ)=∫_{-∞}^{∞} e^{iτx} f_X(x) dx.
The function k_X(τ) is the Fourier transform of f_X(x).
The Fourier transform has an inverse given by f_X(x)= (1/2π)∫_{-∞}^{∞} e^{-iτx} k_X(τ) dτ, suitably interpreted.
Because the characteristic function uniquely determines the density, the mgf, which determines the characteristic function, uniquely determines the density under the hypotheses of Theorem 10.4.
Since X is bounded, its mgf converges for all t, ensuring the above representation is valid and the inversion formula applies.
g_X(t) – moment generating function of X.
k_X(τ) – characteristic function of X, defined as g_X(iτ).
f_X(x) – probability density function of X.
μ_k – the k‑th moment of X.
(i – the imaginary unit, √−1).
Under the assumption that X is bounded, the mgf encodes all information about the distribution; thus knowing the mgf allows one to recover the density uniquely.

The probability of being in state s_j after two steps can be computed by multiplying the transition probabilities of the two steps, i.e., p_{13}^{(2)} = p_{11}p_{13} + p_{12}p_{23} + p_{13}p_{33}.  This is equivalent to taking the dot product of the first row of the transition matrix P with the third column of P, which is precisely the (1,3)-entry of the product P^2.  In general, the entry p_{ij}^{(n)} is obtained by summing over all intermediate states the product of the transition probabilities for the two substeps, which is the (i,j)-entry of P^n.  Thus the theorem reflects that matrix multiplication encodes successive-step transition probabilities.

Let P be the transition matrix of a Markov chain.  The (i,j)-th entry p_{ij}^{(n)} of the matrix P^n gives the probability that the Markov chain, starting in state s_i, will be in state s_j after n steps.
The proof of this theorem is left as an exercise (Exercise 17).

The theorem states that raising the transition matrix to the n-th power yields a matrix whose entries are exactly the probabilities of moving from any state to any other state in n steps, thus providing a direct computational link between matrix powers and multi-step transition probabilities of a Markov chain.

Theorem 11.2 encapsulates the idea that the distribution of states after n steps in a Markov chain is obtained by repeatedly applying the transition matrix to the initial distribution.  Intuitively, multiplying the initial probability vector u by P once gives the distribution after one step, multiplying by P again gives the distribution after two steps, and so forth, so that uPⁿ yields the distribution after n steps.  The i‑th component of the resulting vector is the probability of being in state s_i after n steps.

Let P be the transition matrix of a Markov chain, and let u be the probability vector that represents the starting distribution.  Then the probability that the chain is in state s_i after n steps is the i‑th entry in the vector u^(n) = uPⁿ.

The proof of this theorem is left as an exercise (Exercise 18).  In addition, the text notes that if we want to examine the behavior of the chain under the assumption that it starts in a particular state s_i, we simply choose u to be the probability vector whose i‑th entry equals 1 and all other entries equal 0.  In that case u^(n) gives the exact probabilities of being in each state after n steps when the chain starts in s_i.
