This calculation uses Theorem 11.2 to obtain the distribution after n = 3 steps.  The example explicitly shows the multiplication uP³ and the resulting probabilities for each state.

u – probability vector that represents the starting distribution of states; each entry u_i is the probability that the chain starts in state s_i.  P – transition matrix of the Markov chain; P_{ij} is the probability of transitioning from state s_i to state s_j in one step.  Pⁿ – n-th power of the transition matrix, representing the combined transition probabilities over n successive steps.  u^(n) – probability vector after n steps, defined by u^(n)=uPⁿ; the i‑th entry of u^(n) is the probability that the chain is in state s_i after n steps.

Theorem 11.2 tells us that the state distribution after n steps is fully determined by the initial distribution u and the transition matrix P through the matrix product uPⁿ.  The i‑th component of the resulting vector u^(n) gives the probability that the chain is in state s_i after n steps, regardless of how many intermediate states the chain has visited.  If the chain starts in a single state s_i (i.e., u is the unit vector e_i), then u^(n)=e_iPⁿ and the i‑th row of Pⁿ gives the probabilities of being in each state after n steps.  Thus Theorem 11.2 provides a concise computational rule for evolving the distribution of a Markov chain over time.

The notion that a Markov chain with absorbing states will eventually be absorbed has been a central tenet of stochastic processes since the early 20th century, underpinning models in reliability theory, population genetics, and queueing theory. Theorem 11.3 formalizes this intuition by proving that the probability of absorption is 1 for any absorbing Markov chain.

Every transient state in an absorbing chain has a directed path to at least one absorbing state. Consequently, the chain cannot remain trapped indefinitely among transient states. The probability that the chain has not yet been absorbed after (m) steps decays exponentially with (m), because in each block of (m) steps the chance of remaining transient is at most a fixed constant (p<1). Hence, as the number of steps grows without bound, the probability of still being transient tends to zero, guaranteeing eventual absorption with probability one.
Theorem 11.3: In an absorbing Markov chain, the probability that the process will be absorbed is 1; equivalently, the matrix power (mathbf{Q}^n) converges to the zero matrix as (n	oinfty).

For each transient state (s_j), let (m_j) be the minimal number of steps needed to reach an absorbing state and let (p_j) be the probability that the chain has not reached an absorbing state in (m_j) steps. By construction (p_j<1). Let (m=max_j m_j) and (p=max_j p_j). The probability of not being absorbed in (m) steps is at most (p); in (2m) steps it is at most (p^2); in (ell m) steps it is at most (p^ell). Since (p<1), these probabilities converge to 0 as (ell	oinfty). Because the probability of not being absorbed in (n) steps is monotone decreasing in (n), it follows that (lim_{n	oinfty}mathbf{Q}^n=mathbf{0}), proving the theorem.

In the Drunkard’s Walk example, the transition matrix in canonical form has absorbing states 4 and 5. The chain starts in a transient state (1, 2, or 3). By Theorem 11.3, regardless of the starting transient state, the probability that the drunkard eventually lands on either end of the walk (state 4 or 5) is 1; the process is absorbed almost surely.

( mathbf{P} ) – transition matrix in canonical form; ( mathbf{Q} ) – (t 	imes t) transient‑to‑transient sub‑matrix; ( mathbf{R} ) – (t 	imes r) transient‑to‑absorbing sub‑matrix; ( mathbf{I} ) – identity matrix; ( mathbf{0} ) – zero matrix; ( mathbf{N} ) – fundamental matrix ((mathbf{I}-mathbf{Q})^{-1}); ( mathbf{B} ) – absorption probability matrix (mathbf{N}mathbf{R}); ( mathbf{Q}^n ) – (n)th power of ( mathbf{Q}); ( m_j ) – minimal steps to absorption from state (s_j); ( p_j ) – probability of not being absorbed in (m_j) steps.

Theorem 11.3 guarantees that an absorbing Markov chain will, with probability 1, eventually be absorbed into one of its absorbing states. This result is fundamental for computing absorption probabilities, expected time to absorption, and other long‑term characteristics via the fundamental matrix and the matrix ( mathbf{B} = mathbf{N}mathbf{R} ). It ensures that analyses based on these matrices are well‑defined because they rely on the almost‑sure convergence of the transient dynamics to absorption.

The expected number of steps before absorption, starting from a transient state $s_i$, is denoted $t_i$.  The vector $mathbf{t}$ collects these expectations, with the $i$th entry equal to $t_i$.  For an absorbing Markov chain with fundamental matrix $mathbf{N}=(I-mathbf{Q})^{-1}$ and column vector $mathbf{c}$ whose entries are all one, the relationship $mathbf{t}=mathbf{N}mathbf{c}$ holds.

Theorem 11.5 states that if $mathbf{t}$ is the column vector of expected absorption times $t_i$ and $mathbf{c}$ is a column vector of ones, then $mathbf{t}=mathbf{N}mathbf{c}$, where $mathbf{N}=(I-mathbf{Q})^{-1}$ is the fundamental matrix of the chain.

The expected time to absorption from state $s_i$ equals the expected number of visits to all transient states before absorption.  In the fundamental matrix $mathbf{N}$, the entry $n_{ij}$ counts the expected number of visits to transient state $s_j$ given a start in $s_i$.  Thus the sum of the $i$th row of $mathbf{N}$ is the expected total number of visits to transient states, which is precisely the expected number of steps until absorption from $s_i$.  Writing this for all $i$ simultaneously yields $mathbf{t}$ as the vector of row sums of $mathbf{N}$, and the vector of row sums is $mathbf{N}mathbf{c}$ with $mathbf{c}$ a column of ones.

Absorption probability from a transient state $s_i$ to a particular absorbing state $s_j$ can be viewed as the sum over all possible times $n$ at which the chain first enters $s_j$, weighted by the probability of being in each transient state $s_k$ at time $n$ and then moving to $s_j$ in the next step. The matrix $N$ captures the expected number of visits to each transient state $s_k$ starting from $s_i$, while $R$ gives the one‑step probabilities of jumping from a transient state to each absorbing state. Their product therefore aggregates over all intermediate transient states, yielding the total absorption probability to $s_j$.

Theorem 11.6: Let $b_{ij}$ be the probability that an absorbing Markov chain will be absorbed in the absorbing state $s_j$ if it starts in the transient state $s_i$. Let $B$ be the matrix with entries $b_{ij}$. Then $B$ is a $t$‑by‑$r$ matrix and $B = N R$, where $N = (I - Q)^{-1}$ is the fundamental matrix and $R$ is the transient‑to‑absorbing block of the canonical form of the transition matrix.

The proof proceeds by expanding the definition of $B_{ij}$ as a double sum over all numbers of steps $n$ and intermediate transient states $k$:

$B_{ij} = sum_{n=0}^inftysum_{k=1}^t q_{ik}^{(n)},r_{kj}$. 

Rearranging the sums gives $B_{ij} = sum_{k=1}^t  igl(sum_{n=0}^infty q_{ik}^{(n)} igr) r_{kj}$. The inner sum is precisely $n_{ik}$, the $(i,k)$ entry of the fundamental matrix $N = I+Q+Q^2+cdots = (I-Q)^{-1}$.  Hence $B_{ij} = sum_{k} n_{ik} r_{kj}$, which is the $(i,j)$ entry of the product $N R$. This completes the proof.

The matrix $B$ provides, for every transient state, the probabilities of eventual absorption in each absorbing state. Thus $B$ encapsulates the long‑run behaviour of the chain: given a starting point in the transient region, $B$ tells exactly which absorbing state will be reached and with what probability.

The result is a consequence of the fact that each trial has m equally likely outcomes, so the probability of a particular outcome is 1/m.  A run of k successes can be viewed as a state in a Markov chain where the state number indicates how many consecutive successes have just occurred.  As the chain progresses, the only way to increase the state is to observe the desired outcome, while any other outcome resets the state to 1.  The expected time to absorption (reach state k) therefore grows geometrically with k and m.

The result quantifies how rare long runs of a single outcome are: for example, in a fair coin, the expected number of flips to see nine heads in a row is (2^9-1=511).
It also shows that even though any particular run is unlikely, the long runs expected number of trials is finite and can be computed directly from (m) and (k).

Intuitively, in a fair walk the expected number of steps remaining to reach either absorbing boundary grows quadratically with the distance to the nearest boundary. Starting from a middle point, the walker must take on average a number of steps proportional to the product of distances to each boundary, hence the factor x(n−x).

A function (f) defined on the state space (S) of an absorbing Markov chain is called *harmonic* if it satisfies (f(i)=sum_{jin S}p_{ij}f(j)) for every state (i).  In vector notation this is (mathbf f=mathbf Pmathbf f), where (mathbf P
) is the transition matrix of the chain.

A harmonic function represents a game in which a player's fortune is (f(i)) when the chain is in state (i).  The harmonic condition means that the expected fortune after one step is equal to the fortune before the step, i.e. the game is *fair*.
For a harmonic function (f) we have (mathbf f=mathbf P^nmathbf f) for all integers (nge1).

Let (mathbf P^infty=lim_{n	oinfty}mathbf P^n).  For an absorbing chain this limit exists and has the block form ( egin{pmatrix}mathbf0&mathbf B\mathbf0&mathbf Iend{pmatrix}).  A harmonic function satisfies (mathbf f=mathbf P^inftymathbf f).

If the chain starts in a transient state (i), the expected fortune at absorption is (sum_k b_{ik}f(k)), where (b_{ik}) is the entry of (mathbf B) giving the probability of absorption in absorbing state (k) when starting from (i).  This expected final fortune equals the starting fortune (f(i)).
Thus, in a finite absorbing Markov chain, a fair game defined by a harmonic function remains fair to the end: the expected final fortune equals the initial fortune.

The game of Heads or Tails with an unlimited number of plays is an example where a fair game on an infinite state space does **not** remain fair to the end: starting with one penny and playing until one has two pennies, the gambler is sure to finish one penny ahead.

The waiting time until a specific sequence of outcomes appears in a stochastic experiment can be interpreted as the absorption time in a Markov chain whose states record the current longest suffix of the observed sequence that matches a prefix of the target pattern.  When the chain reaches a state representing the full pattern, the process is absorbed.  This perspective turns the problem of computing expected waiting times into a linear‐algebra problem involving the fundamental matrix of an absorbing Markov chain.

In the case of a run of k identical outcomes, the state is simply the current run length; the chain has absorbing state k.  The expected time to absorption from state 1 is the expected number of trials needed to obtain k consecutive successes.  The linear equations for the expectations reduce to a simple recurrence that yields the closed form (m^k−1)/(m−1).

John Conway's formula appears in the analysis of the Penney‑ante game, a non‑transitive coin‑tossing game first described by W. Penney in 1969. The formula was popularised by Martin Gardner in his 1974 Scientific American column “Mathematical Games” and is attributed to John Conway, who derived a simple expression for the odds that the first player’s pattern beats the second player’s pattern.

The formula arises from comparing the expected waiting times for the two competing patterns. By treating each pattern as a “gamble” that pays an amount equal to the expected waiting time (BB for pattern B, AA for pattern A) and using the linearity of expectation together with the fact that the total expected time until one of the patterns appears can be written in two ways—once conditioned on the first player winning and once on the second player winning—the odds emerge as a ratio of differences of these expected payouts.

For two distinct patterns A and B (neither a subpattern of the other) in the Penney‑ante game, the odds that the first player’s pattern A occurs before the second player’s pattern B are given by John Conway’s formula: 

p_A / p_B = (BB – BA) / (AA – AB),

where p_A is the probability that A wins, p_B=1‑p_A, AA and BB are the expected waiting times (or “pay‑offs”) when the game is played for pattern A alone or pattern B alone, and AB, BA are the expected amounts earned by a gambler who starts while pattern A (respectively B) has just appeared and then continues until pattern B (respectively A) occurs.

Starting from the gambler interpretation, the expected time to reach pattern B can be decomposed as 

BB = E(T^{A or B}) + p_A·(BB – AB),

because with probability p_A the first pattern to appear is A, after which an additional expected time of BB – AB remains until B appears. Interchanging the roles of A and B yields 

AA = E(T^{A or B}) + p_B·(AA – BA).

Subtracting the two equations eliminates the unknown E(T^{A or B}) and using p_A + p_B = 1 gives a linear system in p_A and p_B. Solving the system yields 

p_A / p_B = (BB – BA) / (AA – AB),

which is precisely Conway’s formula.

When the patterns have length k = 2, the quantities satisfy AA – AB = BB – BA, so the ratio equals 1 and the game is fair (p_A = p_B = ½). For length k = 3, the differences are never equal; for instance, if A=HTH and B=HHT, one finds BB – BA ≠ AA – AB, giving p_A < ½. Hence the second player always has a winning advantage for any choice of A when k = 3, as predicted by Conway’s formula.

Conway’s formula translates the combinatorial structure of the two patterns into a simple odds ratio. The numerator (BB – BA) measures how much longer it typically takes to see B after a B‑start compared to after an A‑start, while the denominator (AA – AB) measures the analogous difference for A. A larger numerator relative to the denominator means pattern A is less likely to win, giving the second player a strategic advantage. The formula thus provides an immediate way to compute optimal strategies in Penney‑ante without solving full Markov‑chain equations.

The relationship (mathbf{B}=mathbf{N}mathbf{R}) is a classical result in the theory of absorbing Markov chains and appears in many standard texts on stochastic processes. It provides a convenient computational tool for finding absorption probabilities and expected absorption times. The theorem is often associated with the work of Kemeny and Snell in the 1960s, although the underlying concepts were developed earlier by Markov and Kolmogorov. The specific derivation presented here follows the style of standard proofs that express the absorption probabilities in terms of the fundamental matrix and the transition sub‑matrix to absorbing states.

The absorption probability from a given transient state is built recursively: either the chain moves directly into the absorbing state in the next step (captured by (mathbf{R})), or it first moves to another transient state and then eventually gets absorbed (captured by (mathbf{Q}mathbf{B})). The matrix identity rearranges this recursive relationship into a closed‑form solution, where the inverse ((mathbf{I}-mathbf{Q})^{-1}) sums over all possible numbers of visits to transient states. This mirrors the idea that the total probability of absorption is the sum over all possible sequences of transient steps leading into an absorbing state.

In an absorbing Markov chain, let the state space be partitioned into transient states (s_i) and absorbing states (s_j). Define (b_{ij}) to be the probability that, starting from transient state (s_i), the chain is eventually absorbed in absorbing state (s_j). Let (p_{ij}) denote the one‑step transition probability from (s_i) to (s_j). The theorem states that the matrix (mathbf{B}=(b_{ij})) of absorption probabilities satisfies the linear system (mathbf{B}=mathbf{N}mathbf{R}), where (mathbf{N}=(mathbf{I}-mathbf{Q})^{-1}) is the fundamental matrix and (mathbf{R}) contains the transition probabilities from transient to absorbing states.

Starting from any transient state (s_i), the probability of eventual absorption in (s_j) satisfies the recursive relation (displaystyle b_{ij}=p_{ij}+sum_k p_{ik}b_{kj}), where the sum extends over all transient states (s_k). Writing this system for all transient states produces the matrix equation (mathbf{B}=mathbf{P}_{	ext{TA}}+mathbf{Q}mathbf{B}), where (mathbf{Q}) is the sub‑matrix of (mathbf{P}) containing transitions among transient states and (mathbf{P}_{	ext{TA}}) is the sub‑matrix of (mathbf{P}) containing transitions from transient to absorbing states, i.e. (mathbf{R}). Rearranging gives ((mathbf{I}-mathbf{Q})mathbf{B}=mathbf{R}). Since (mathbf{I}-mathbf{Q}) is nonsingular for an absorbing chain, its inverse (mathbf{N}=(mathbf{I}-mathbf{Q})^{-1}) exists, and multiplying both sides by (mathbf{N}) yields the desired identity (mathbf{B}=mathbf{N}mathbf{R}).

Consider the Gambler’s Ruin chain on states ({0,1,dots,N}) where states (0) and (N) are absorbing. The transition matrix (mathbf{Q}) contains probabilities (p) and (q) for moving between the (N-1) transient states. The matrix (mathbf{R}) has non‑zero entries only for transitions from the boundary transient states (1) and (N-1) to the absorbing states (0) and (N). Applying (mathbf{B}=mathbf{N}mathbf{R}) recovers the well‑known absorption probabilities (b_{iN}= rac{i}{N}) when (p=q) or (b_{iN}= rac{(q/p)^i-1}{(q/p)^N-1}) when (p
eq q).

(s_i) – transient state, (s_j) – absorbing state; (p_{ij}) – one‑step transition probability from (s_i) to (s_j); (b_{ij}) – probability of eventual absorption in (s_j) starting from (s_i); (mathbf{Q}) – transition matrix restricted to transient states; (mathbf{R}) – transition matrix from transient to absorbing states; (mathbf{I}) – identity matrix; (mathbf{N}=(mathbf{I}-mathbf{Q})^{-1}) – fundamental matrix.

The equation (mathbf{B}=mathbf{N}mathbf{R}) expresses that the overall absorption probability from a transient state is the sum over all possible paths of a single step into a transient state followed by eventual absorption, weighted by the expected number of visits to each transient state. The fundamental matrix (mathbf{N}) counts expected visits to each transient state before absorption, while (mathbf{R}) records the chance of moving directly from a transient state into a specific absorbing state. Thus (mathbf{B}) is obtained by weighting the one‑step absorption probabilities by the expected visit counts.

The martingale system theorem is rooted in the theory of martingales developed in probability theory in the early 20th century.  Its application to gambling was popularized in the 1960s and 1970s, notably in Penney’s work on non‑transitive games and in later analyses of pattern‑matching problems such as those presented by Li.  The theorem provides a rigorous foundation for the intuitive “fairness” of games where each bet is a zero‑expected‑value gamble.

The theorem captures the intuitive idea that in a game where every bet is fair, the player cannot expect to win or lose money on average. Therefore, the expected number of tosses needed to hit a target pattern (which determines how long the game lasts) is precisely the same as the expected payout the casino must make, because any surplus or deficit would contradict fairness.

The Martingale system theorem states that in a fair gambling system modeled as a martingale, the expected net gain of the gamblers after any number of plays is zero. In the context of pattern‑matching coin tosses, this implies that the expected time $T^B$ to first observe a pattern $B$ equals the expected total payout $BB$ that the casino must pay to gamblers who win when $B$ occurs.

Li employed the martingale theorem to argue that because all bets are fair (each bet has expected value zero), the expected net change in the gamblers’ fortunes is zero. Thus the expected amount of money the casino collects, $E(T^B)$, must equal the expected amount it pays out, $BB$. This argument is equivalent to showing that the gambler’s fortune process is a martingale and applying the optional stopping theorem at the stopping time when pattern $B$ first appears.

1. For $B=	ext{HTH}$ the martingale argument yields $E(T^{	ext{HTH}})=BB=10$; hence the expected number of tosses until the first appearance of HTH is 10. 2. For $B=	ext{HHH}$ we have $BB=14$, so $E(T^{	ext{HHH}})=14$. 3. When starting from pattern $A=	ext{HT}$ and seeking $B=	ext{HTH}$, the gambler’s expected remaining time is $E_A(T^B)=BB-AB=10-4=6$, again consistent with the martingale reasoning.

$T^B$ – random time until the first occurrence of pattern $B$.  $BB$ – total payout to gamblers who win when pattern $B$ occurs.  $AB$ – total amount gamblers win when they arrive during the occurrence of pattern $A$.  $E(cdot)$ – expected value operator.  The notation $E(T^B)=BB$ expresses the equality derived from the martingale property.

The equality $E(T^B)=BB$ demonstrates that the expected duration of the game (number of tosses until the target pattern appears) and the expected financial outlay to gamblers are directly linked through the martingale property.  This relation allows one to compute expected waiting times for patterns by determining the payout structure of the associated gambling scheme, or conversely, to verify the fairness of a betting scheme by checking that the expected payout equals the expected number of trials.

Theorem 11.7 relies on the observation that each application of the transition matrix to a vector performs an averaging operation on the vector’s components.  Repeated averaging drives the maximum component down and the minimum component up, so the difference between the largest and smallest entries of µ_n=µP^n decreases to zero.  Consequently the sequence of vectors P^nµ converges to a constant vector for every initial vector µ, which forces every row of P^n to become identical as n grows.

Theorem 11.7 – For a regular transition matrix P the sequence of powers P^n converges, as n→∞, to a limiting matrix W whose all rows are equal to a strictly positive probability vector w (i.e., w has strictly positive components and the components sum to 1).

Theorem 11.8 – Let W=lim_{n→∞}P^n, let w be the common row of W, and let c be the column vector of all ones. (a) wP=w and any row vector v with vP=v is a scalar multiple of w. (b) Pc=c and any column vector x with Px=x is a scalar multiple of c.

The fixed vector theorem captures the idea that in a regular Markov chain the long-term behavior is independent of the starting state; after many steps the probability distribution over states converges to a single vector w.  This vector is called a fixed row vector because it is unchanged by multiplication on the right by the transition matrix P (wP = w).  Likewise, a fixed column vector is unchanged by multiplication on the left (Px = x).  The theorem shows that such fixed vectors are unique up to a scalar multiple and, for the row vector, the only unit-sum multiple is the limiting distribution w.  The theorem therefore explains why the steady-state probabilities exist and are unique for regular chains.

For a regular transition matrix P the limit W = lim_{n→∞}P^n exists and every row of W is identical; denote that common row by w.  The vector w satisfies wP = w, and any row vector v with vP = v is a scalar multiple of w.  Moreover, Pc = c where c is the all‑ones column vector, and any column vector x with Px = x is a scalar multiple of c.

Since P is regular, P^n → W as n→∞.  Multiplying by P, P^{n+1} = P^n P → W P.  But P^{n+1} also converges to W, so W = W P, giving wP = w.  If vP = v, then v = vP^n for all n, and taking limits yields v = vW = r w where r is the sum of the components of v, so v is a scalar multiple of w.  For the column vectors, Px = x implies x = P^n x, hence x = W x.  Since W has identical rows, W x has all equal components, so x is a scalar multiple of the all‑ones vector c.  Thus the only fixed row (up to scaling) is w and the only fixed column (up to scaling) is c.

Since the left nullspace of P‑I is one‑dimensional, any two left eigenvectors associated with eigenvalue 1 must be scalar multiples of each other; normalizing to sum to 1 yields a unique probability vector, giving a clear geometric picture of a single direction in the row‑space that remains invariant under the transition dynamics.
The theorem reflects that in an ergodic (irreducible and aperiodic) Markov chain every state communicates with every other, forcing any invariant vector to assign the same weight to all states.

Theorem 11.8 states that for a regular (or ergodic) transition matrix P, the left nullspace of the matrix P‑I has dimension 1, equivalently there is a unique fixed row probability vector w satisfying wP=w.
If P is the transition matrix of an ergodic Markov chain and x is a column vector satisfying Px = x, then all components of x are equal; i.e., x is a constant vector.

The text does not give a detailed proof of Theorem 11.8; it merely cites the result and notes that the left nullspace of P‑I being one‑dimensional implies the uniqueness of the fixed row vector. The proof for ergodic chains is indicated to follow from the fact that an ergodic transition matrix can be written as a convex combination (½I+½P) that is regular and has the same fixed vectors.

Assume x satisfies Px = x and let M = max_i x_i with x_k = M for some index k. If p_{kj}>0 then from the equality (Px)_k = Σ_j p_{kj} x_j = M we deduce that every x_j with p_{kj}>0 must also equal M. By ergodicity, for any state i there exists a path of positive‑probability transitions from k to i, and iterating the previous argument shows x_i = M for all i. Hence x is constant.

In a regular chain, the unique stationary distribution has strictly positive entries, which is a special case of Theorem 11.8.

The theorem guarantees that a regular or ergodic Markov chain possesses exactly one stationary (fixed) row probability vector, which is strictly positive. This vector is the unique solution of wP=w and provides the long‑run distribution of the chain regardless of the initial state.
The theorem guarantees that the only eigenvectors associated with eigenvalue 1 for an ergodic chain are multiples of the all‑ones vector, implying a unique stationary distribution up to scaling.
Consequently, any invariant probability distribution must assign positive probability to every state.

Theorem 11.9 generalizes the convergence result for a regular Markov chain to the case where the initial state is not a single state but an arbitrary probability vector v. It states that, regardless of the starting distribution, the distribution after many steps converges to the unique stationary distribution w, provided the chain is regular. This reflects the idea that the long–run behavior of a regular Markov chain is independent of its starting distribution.

Theorem 11.10 extends the earlier result of Theorem 11.8, which was proved only for regular Markov chains, to the more general class of ergodic chains. It also relies on the observation that for any ergodic transition matrix P, the convex combination $ ar{P}= rac12I+ rac12P$ is a regular transition matrix that has exactly the same fixed vectors as P, a fact that is proved in Exercises 25–28.

In an ergodic chain every state is visited infinitely often, so the long‑run proportion of time spent in each state must be strictly positive. The theorem shows that there is exactly one such probability vector w that satisfies $wP=w$, and that no other row vector can remain unchanged under P unless it is a scalar multiple of w. The fact that any right eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 is constant reflects that the chain has no nontrivial recurrent substructures and all states are essentially equivalent in the limit.

For an ergodic Markov chain there exists a unique probability vector $w$ such that $wP=w$ and all components of $w$ are strictly positive. Moreover, any row vector $v$ with $vP=v$ is a scalar multiple of $w$, and any column vector $x$ satisfying $Px=x$ is a constant vector.

The proof follows directly from Theorem 11.8 applied to the regular matrix $ ar{P}=	frac12I+	frac12P$. Since $ ar{P}$ has the same fixed vectors as $P$, the existence and uniqueness of the strictly positive stationary row vector for regular chains carries over to all ergodic chains. The properties about row and column eigenvectors then follow from the one‑dimensionality of the left nullspace of $P-I$ and the fact that the only right eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 is the all‑ones vector. ∎

The Land of Oz weather chain is ergodic; Theorem 11.10 guarantees its unique stationary distribution $w=(0.4,0.2,0.4)$, which is strictly positive and to which any initial distribution converges. In Example 11.22, the nine‑state maze is ergodic but not regular; the theorem still ensures a unique strictly positive stationary distribution for its transition matrix, and that any invariant row vector is a multiple of this distribution.

$w$ – the unique stationary probability row vector; $P$ – the transition matrix of the Markov chain; $I$ – the identity matrix; $v$ – an arbitrary row vector; $x$ – an arbitrary column vector; $wP=w$ expresses that $w$ is a left eigenvector of $P$ with eigenvalue 1.

Theorem 11.10 formalizes the long‑run stability of finite ergodic Markov chains: there is exactly one stationary distribution, and it assigns a positive probability to every state, reflecting the chain’s ability to reach all states from any starting state. Any row vector that remains unchanged after applying $P$ must be proportional to this stationary vector, so the stationary distribution is unique up to scaling. The statement that any column eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 is constant underscores that the chain’s equilibrium behaviour is the same from every starting state; the all‑ones column vector is the only right eigenvector associated with the eigenvalue 1, which is a standard consequence of ergodicity.

Theorem 11.11 is presented in section 11.3, following the discussion of Theorem 11.10 which establishes the uniqueness of the fixed probability vector w for ergodic chains.  It extends the results about regular Markov chains to all ergodic chains.
The fixed probability vector $mathbf{w}$ of a Markov chain can be interpreted as the proportion of time the process spends in each state in the long run.

Theorem 1.7 is referenced in the discussion following Lemma 11.1, indicating that it deals with the fact that each entry of the vector P y is a weighted average of the entries of y. This observation is used to bound the spread of the components of P y relative to y.

The key idea behind Theorem 1.7 is that when a transition matrix P is applied to a column vector y, the resulting vector’s components are convex combinations (weighted averages) of the components of y. This property implies that the spread between the largest and smallest components can only shrink or stay the same, which is the foundation of convergence arguments for Markov chains.

Theorem 1.7: For a transition matrix P, every entry of the product P y is a weighted average of the entries of y, where the weights are the corresponding row entries of P and sum to 1. Consequently, the maximum component of P y cannot exceed the maximum component of y, and the minimum component of P y cannot be below the minimum component of y.

The proof appears in the discussion following Theorem 1.7. It observes that each entry of P y is a linear combination of the entries of y with non‑negative coefficients that sum to 1, i.e., a convex combination or weighted average. By selecting the extreme cases where all but one component of y equals the maximum M₀ and one component equals the minimum m₀, the largest possible value of a component of P y is bounded above by d m₀ + (1–d) M₀, where d is the smallest entry of P. Similarly, the smallest possible value is bounded below by d M₀ + (1–d) m₀. This leads to the inequality M₁ – m₁ ≤ (1 – 2d)(M₀ – m₀), showing that the spread decreases or remains unchanged.

No specific numerical example is given in the text, but the proof discusses an extreme scenario where all but one component of y equals M₀ and the remaining component equals m₀, illustrating how the weighted average bounds the new components.

d := the smallest entry of the transition matrix P. M₀ := the maximum component of the vector y. m₀ := the minimum component of the vector y. M₁ := the maximum component of P y. m₁ := the minimum component of P y. y := any column vector of dimension r. P := an r × r transition matrix.

Theorem 1.7 provides a quantitative way to understand how applying a transition matrix contracts the spread of a vector’s components. This contraction property underlies the convergence of regular Markov chains to a unique stationary distribution, as shown in the subsequent fundamental limit theorem for regular chains.

The lemma captures a key contraction property of a stochastic matrix with all strictly positive entries: when it acts on any vector, the spread between the largest and smallest components shrinks by at least a factor of (1‑2d), where d is the smallest transition probability. This observation underpins the convergence of powers of a regular Markov transition matrix to a rank‑one matrix whose rows are all identical.

Let P be an r‑by‑r transition matrix with no zero entries. Let d be the smallest entry of the matrix. Let y be a column vector with r components, the largest of which is M0 and the smallest m0. Let M1 and m1 be the largest and smallest component, respectively, of the vector Py. Then M1 - m1 ≤ (1 - 2d)(M0 - m0).

In the discussion following Theorem 1.7, it was noted that each entry in the vector Py is a weighted average of the entries in y. The largest weighted average that could be obtained in the present case would occur if all but one of the entries of y have value M0 and one entry has value m0, and this one small entry is weighted by the smallest possible weight, namely d. In this case, the weighted average would equal dm0 + (1 - d)M0. Similarly, the smallest possible weighted average equals dM0 + (1 - d)m0. Thus, M1 - m1 ≤ (dm0 + (1 - d)M0) - (dM0 + (1 - d)m0) = (1 - 2d)(M0 - m0).
P – r‑by‑r transition matrix with no zero entries
d – the smallest entry of P
y – arbitrary column vector of length r
M0 – maximum component of y
m0 – minimum component of y
M1 – maximum component of Py
m1 – minimum component of Py

The lemma demonstrates that applying a strictly positive stochastic matrix pulls any vector’s components closer together. The factor (1‑2d) is strictly less than 1 because d>0, so repeated application forces the vector toward a constant vector. This contraction property is essential in proving that the powers of a regular transition matrix converge to a matrix with identical rows, the fundamental limit theorem for regular Markov chains.

The theorem was first proved by W. Doeblin in 1937 ("Exposé de la Théorie des Chaînes Simples Constantes de Markov à un Nombre Fin de États"). Doeblin’s coupling argument is a seminal contribution to the theory of Markov chains and the concept of convergence to a stationary distribution.

Regularity guarantees that, after enough steps, the Markov chain has a positive probability of reaching any state from any starting state. By coupling the chain started in an arbitrary state with a copy started in the stationary distribution, the two chains almost surely meet after a finite random time. Once they meet, their future trajectories are identical, forcing the distributions to coalesce. This explains why the limiting distribution is independent of the initial state.
Let **P** be the transition matrix for a regular Markov chain with fixed vector **w**. Then for any initial probability vector **u**, the row vector **u** **P**ⁿ converges to **w** as **n**→∞.

Let X₀, X₁,… be a Markov chain with transition matrix **P** started in state sᵢ and let Y₀, Y₁,… be an independent chain with the same matrix **P** started with initial probabilities given by **w**. Construct the joint chain **P*** on state pairs (s_k,s_l) with transition probabilities **P***((k,l),(i,j))=P(k,i)P(l,j). Since **P** is regular, there exists N such that **P**^N(i,j)>0 for all i,j; hence **P*** is also regular and any pair can be reached from any other pair in at most N steps. Let T be the first time the two chains meet, i.e. X_T=Y_T. Then P(T>n)→0. For any n≥T, X_n and Y_n are in the same state, so P(X_n=j|n≥T)=P(Y_n=j|n≥T). Multiplying by P(n≥T) yields P(X_n=j,n≥T)=P(Y_n=j,n≥T). Since Y_n has distribution **w** for every n, the second term tends to w_j and the first term tends to w_j as well. The difference between P(X_n=j,n≥T) and P(X_n=j) is bounded by P(n<T), which tends to 0; thus P(X_n=j)→w_j for each j. Therefore **u** **P**ⁿ→**w**.

Consider the 2×2 regular transition matrix P=⎡0.5 0.5; 0.25 0.75⎤. Its stationary distribution is w=(2/3, 1/3). For any initial distribution u, the product u Pⁿ converges to w; e.g., u=(1,0) gives Pⁿu→(2/3, 1/3) as n→∞.

**P** – transition matrix of the Markov chain (r×r), 
**u** – initial row probability vector, 
**w** – stationary distribution satisfying **w** **P** = **w**, 
X_n – state of the first chain at time n, 
Y_n – state of the second chain at time n, 
**P*** – joint transition matrix on ordered pairs (s_i,s_j), 
T – first time X_T = Y_T.

The theorem asserts that a regular Markov chain is ergodic: its long-run behavior is completely determined by a unique stationary distribution **w**, regardless of how the chain starts. The mean recurrence time $r_i$ measures the expected number of steps a Markov chain, started in state $s_i$, must take before it returns to $s_i$ for the first time. Because the chain is ergodic, a return is guaranteed, and the quantity captures how often the chain revisits a state on average.

For an ergodic Markov chain, the mean recurrence time for state $s_i$ is $r_i = 1/w_i$, where $w_i$ is the $i$‑th component of the fixed (stationary) probability vector $\mathbf w$ of the transition matrix.

Multiplying the matrix equation $(\mathbf I-\mathbf P)\mathbf M = \mathbf C-\mathbf D$ (Equation 11.6) on the right by the stationary row vector $\mathbf w$ and using $\mathbf w(\mathbf I-\mathbf P)=\mathbf 0$ gives $\mathbf w\mathbf C-\mathbf w\mathbf D=\mathbf 0$. Since $\mathbf w\mathbf C$ is a row vector of all ones and $\mathbf w\mathbf D$ has entries $w_i r_i$, we obtain $(1,1,\dots,1) = (w_1 r_1, w_2 r_2,\dots,w_n r_n)$. Equating components yields $w_i r_i =1$, i.e. $r_i = 1/w_i$ for each state $s_i$.

In the maze example (Example 11.25) the stationary vector is $\mathbf w = (\tfrac{1}{12},\tfrac{1}{8},\tfrac{1}{12},\tfrac{1}{8},\tfrac{1}{6},\tfrac{1}{8},\tfrac{1}{12},\tfrac{1}{8},\tfrac{1}{12})$. Hence the mean recurrence times are the reciprocals: $\mathbf r = (12,8,12,8,6,8,12,8,12)$.
For a weather model of the Land of Oz with stationary vector $\mathbf w=(2/5,1/5,2/5)$, the mean number of days between rainy days is $5/2$, between nice days is $5$, and between snowy days is $5/2$.

The Mean First Passage Matrix Theorem appears in Section 11.5 of a standard Markov‑chain textbook, following the development of the fundamental matrix $Z=(I-P+W)^{-1}$ for ergodic chains. It is presented as Theorem 11.16 and builds on earlier lemmas concerning the properties of $Z$, $W$, and the stationary row vector $w$.

The theorem shows that the expected number of steps needed to go from state $i$ to state $j$ (the mean first‑passage time $m_{ij}$) can be read directly from the fundamental matrix $Z$. The entry $z_{jj}$ measures the total expected time spent in state $j$ starting from the stationary distribution, while $z_{ij}$ measures the same quantity when the chain starts in state $i$. Subtracting $z_{ij}$ from $z_{jj}$ isolates the extra waiting time caused by starting away from $j$, and dividing by the stationary probability $w_j$ normalises this by the long‑run frequency of visits to $j$.

For an ergodic Markov chain with transition matrix $P$, stationary row vector $w$, and fundamental matrix $Z=(I-P+W)^{-1}$, the mean first‑passage matrix $M$ is given entrywise by
$$m_{ij}=\frac{z_{jj}-z_{ij}}{w_j},\qquad i,j=1,\dots,n,$$
where $z_{ij}$ denotes the $(i,j)$ entry of $Z$ and $w_j$ is the $j$‑th component of $w$.

The proof starts from the identity $(I-P)M=C-D$ (Equation 11.6) and left‑multiplies by $Z$, using Lemma 11.2 which gives $Z(I-P)=I-W$ and $Zw=w$. This yields $M-WM=C-ZD$. Solving for the $(i,j)$ entry gives $m_{ij}=1-z_{ij}r_j+(wM)_j$, where $r_j=1/w_j$. Setting $i=j$ and using $m_{jj}=0$ gives $(wM)_j=z_{jj}r_j-1$. Substituting this back into the expression for $m_{ij}$ eliminates $(wM)_j$ and yields $m_{ij}=(z_{jj}-z_{ij})r_j$, i.e. $m_{ij}=(z_{jj}-z_{ij})/w_j$. The derivation relies only on the properties $Zc=c$, $wZ=w$, and $Z(I-P)=I-W$ established in Lemma 11.2.

In the “Land of Oz’’ example the transition matrix $P$ and stationary matrix $W$ are given, leading to
$$Z=\begin{pmatrix} 86/75 & 1/25 & -14/75\\ 2/25 & 21/25 & 2/25\\ -14/75 & 1/25 & 86/75\end{pmatrix},\qquad w=(2/5,\,1/5,\,2/5).$$
Applying the theorem, for instance
$$m_{12}=\frac{z_{22}-z_{12}}{w_2}=\frac{21/25-1/25}{1/5}=4,$$
and similarly computing all entries gives
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 4 & 10/3\\ 8/3 & 0 & 8/3\\ 10/3 & 4 & 0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Each entry $m_{ij}$ of $M$ is the expected number of steps the chain, started in state $i$, will take before it visits state $j$ for the first time. The formula shows that this expectation depends only on two quantities from the fundamental matrix: the diagonal entry $z_{jj}$, which captures the average cumulative time the chain spends in $j$ when started from the stationary distribution, and the off‑diagonal entry $z_{ij}$, which captures the same cumulative time when starting from $i$. The division by $w_j$ adjusts for how frequently state $j$ is visited in the long run, converting cumulative time differences into a first‑passage expectation.

Markov introduced Markov chains as an extension of independent random variables, and in a later paper proved a central limit theorem for chains with positive transition probabilities and numerical states. The theorem states that for such chains the normalized number of visits to any fixed state converges in distribution to the standard normal, regardless of the initial state. This result provides the foundation for applying normal approximation to long‑run frequencies in Markov processes.

The chain visits each state a fraction w_j of the time in the long run. The count S_j^{(n)} of visits to state s_j over n steps behaves like a sum of n dependent indicator variables with mean w_j. The ergodic mixing of the chain weakens the dependence sufficiently that the classical central limit behaviour emerges, yielding an approximately normal distribution for the scaled deviation from the mean.

For an ergodic Markov chain with fixed probability row vector w and for any state s_j, the random variable × S_j^{(n)} - n w_j over ± sqrt{n σ_j^2} converges in distribution to a standard normal: “P! ig(r < (S_j^{(n)}-n w_j)/±sqrt{n σ_j^2} < s”)	o  rac{1}{sqrt{2π}}int_r^s e^{-x^2/2}dx” as n→∞, for any choice of starting state, where σ_j^2 = 2 w_j z_{jj} - w_j - w_j^2.

The proof proceeds by first establishing that E[S_j^{(n)}]=n w_j+o(n) for an ergodic chain. Next, one shows that the asymptotic variance of S_j^{(n)} equals σ_j^2 n+o(n) using the fundamental matrix of the chain, where z_{jj} denotes the jth diagonal entry of the deviation matrix. With these two asymptotic moments in hand, a martingale or mixing‑CLT argument for Markov chains shows that the standardized sum converges to a standard normal distribution as n→∞, independently of the starting state.

In the Ehrenfest urn model with 2n balls, the equilibrium probability of having i balls in the first urn is w_i = Δ{2n}{i}/2^{2n}. For a fixed i, the random variable S_i^{(n)} counts the number of times the chain visits state i over n steps. By the central limit theorem for Markov chains, the normalized variable (S_i^{(n)}-n w_i)/±sqrt{n σ_i^2} converges to a standard normal as n→∞, where σ_i^2 is computed from the deviation matrix of the Ehrenfest transition matrix.

S_j^{(n)}: total number of visits to state s_j during the first n steps; w_j: jth component of the fixed probability row vector w (the equilibrium distribution); σ_j^2: asymptotic variance per step defined by σ_j^2 = 2 w_j z_{jj} - w_j - w_j^2; z_{jj}: jth diagonal entry of the deviation matrix Z = (I-P+1ρ)^{-1}; P: transition matrix; I: identity matrix; ρ: stationary distribution row vector.

The theorem tells us that, for large n, the proportion of time the chain spends in any particular state is tightly concentrated around its equilibrium probability w_j, and the fluctuations around this mean are normally distributed with variance proportional to n. This allows practitioners to approximate the distribution of long‑run frequencies and to assess probabilities of extreme deviations using normal tables, even when the chain exhibits strong dependence between successive states.

For an ergodic Markov chain, the weighted sum of mean first passage times from state i to all states j, weighted by the stationary distribution w_j, equals the sum of the diagonal entries of the fundamental matrix Z minus 1, which is a constant K independent of i.

A walk of length $2m$ that ends at the origin must have exactly $m$ upward steps and $m$ downward steps.  The number of distinct sequences of $m$ up‑steps and $m$ down‑steps is $ inom{2m}{m}$, and each of the $2^{2m}$ possible step sequences is equally likely.  Thus the probability that a random walk of $2m$ steps returns to the origin is the ratio of favorable paths to total paths, yielding $u_{2m}= inom{2m}{m}/2^{2m}$.  The impossibility of returning at an odd step follows from the parity of the walk: each step changes the position by $pm1$, so after an odd number of steps the position cannot be zero.

The probability of a return to the origin at an even time $2m$ in a simple symmetric random walk is given by $u_{2m}= inom{2m}{m}2^{-2m}$.  The probability of a return to the origin at any odd time is zero.
No explicit proof of Theorem 12.1 is provided in the supplied text; the statement is presented without derivation.  The result is later used as a foundational identity for subsequent arguments.

The factor $2^{-2m}$ represents the probability of any particular sequence of $2m$ independent $pm1$ steps, each with probability $1/2$.

Theorem 12.1 gives the exact combinatorial probability for a symmetric random walk to be at the origin after an even number of steps.  It forms the basis for later derivations of first‑return probabilities ($f_{2m}$), generating‑function identities, and the study of eventual return probabilities in higher dimensions.
The theorem is presented without explicit historical attribution; it appears as a basic combinatorial identity in the study of symmetric random walks.

Any walk that ends at the origin after 2n steps can be uniquely broken at its first visit to the origin. The probability of the initial segment is f_{2k} and the probability of completing the walk from that point is u_{2n-2k}. Adding over all possible k yields the total probability u_{2n}.
For n \ge 1, the probabilities \{u_{2k}\} and \{f_{2k}\} satisfy the relation u_{2n}=f_{0}u_{2n}+f_{2}u_{2n-2}+\cdots+f_{2n}u_{0}.
Theorem 12.2 provides an example of a recursion that relates the (m)th term in an unknown sequence to earlier terms in the same sequence and to terms of one or more known sequences.

The proof counts the total number of paths of length 2n that start and end at the origin, which is u_{2n}2^{2n}. Each such path is uniquely classified by the time 2k (0\le k\le n) of its first return to the origin. For a fixed k, the initial segment from (0,0) to (2k,0) is a first‑return path, occurring with probability f_{2k} and having 2^{2k} possible realizations; the remaining segment from (2k,0) to (2n,0) is an unrestricted return path, occurring with probability u_{2n-2k} and having 2^{2n-2k} realizations. Hence the number of paths with first return at time 2k is f_{2k}2^{2k}\,u_{2n-2k}2^{2n-2k}=f_{2k}u_{2n-2k}2^{2n}. Summing over k yields u_{2n}2^{2n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}f_{2k}u_{2n-2k}2^{2n}. Dividing both sides by 2^{2n} gives the stated equation.

The right‑hand side is precisely the discrete convolution of the sequences \{f_{2k}\} and \{u_{2k}\}. In generating‑function terms this yields the relation U(x)=1+U(x)F(x), where U and F are the ordinary generating functions of \{u_{2n}\} and \{f_{2n}\} respectively.

Theorem 12.3 was introduced in Chapter 12 as an application of generating‑function techniques to random‑walk problems, following the earlier development in Theorem 12.2 and Example 12.1. The proof begins by defining the ordinary generating functions $U(x)=sum_{m=0}^infty u_{2m}x^m$ and $F(x)=sum_{m=0}^infty f_{2m}x^m$.  From Theorem 12.2 one obtains the functional equation $U(x)=1+U(x)F(x)$ (equation 12.1).  Solving for $F(x)$ gives $F(x)= rac{U(x)-1}{U(x)}$.  Using Theorem 12.1, $U(x)=sum_{mge0} inom{2m}{m}2^{-2m}x^m= rac1{sqrt{1-x}}$.  Substituting into the expression for $F(x)$ yields $F(x)=1-(1-x)^{1/2}$.  Expanding $(1-x)^{1/2}$ by the binomial theorem and extracting the coefficient of $x^m$ leads to $f_{2m}= rac{u_{2m-2}}{2m}= rac{ inom{2m-2}{m-1}}{m2^{2m-1}}= rac{ inom{2m}{m}}{(2m-1)2^{2m}}= rac{u_{2m}}{2m-1}$, which completes the proof.

Setting $m=1$ gives $f_{2}=  rac{ inom{2}{1}}{(3)2^{2}}= rac{2}{12}= rac{1}{6}$, confirming that the probability of first return at time 2 is $1/6$. The distribution formula was first recorded by W. Feller in *Introduction to Probability Theory and its Applications* (3rd ed., 1968). The connection between $E(M_n)$ and the expected number of equalizations was noted in the same text (Exercise 9).

Because a simple random walk fluctuates like $\sqrt{n}$, the most probable maximal height grows on the order of $\sqrt{n}$. The asymptotic formula $E(M_n)\sim\sqrt{2/\pi}\sqrt{n}$ reflects this diffusion scaling and matches the asymptotics for the expected number of equalizations.

Let $M_n=max_{0\le k\le n}S_k$ be the maximum of a simple symmetric random walk of length $n$. For $r\ge0$ define $p_{n,r}=\binom{n}{(n+r)/2}2^{-n}$. Then the distribution of $M_n$ is
$$P(M_n=r)=\begin{cases}p_{n,r},&r\equiv n\pmod 2,\\ p_{n,r+1},&r\not\equiv n\pmod 2.\end{cases}$$

The proof follows from the ballot‑type argument that a walk ending at height $r$ and never falling below zero must have the same number of up‑steps as down‑steps except for the excess $r$; counting such paths yields $p_{n,r}$ when the parity matches, and $p_{n,r+1}$ otherwise. A detailed combinatorial derivation is given in Feller (1968), Example 12.3.
Using the asymptotic $\binom{2m}{m}\sim\frac{2^{2m}}{\sqrt{\pi m}}$, the formulas give $E(M_n)\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\sqrt{n}$ as $n\to\infty$.

The theorem describes exactly how likely the walk is to achieve a given maximal height $r$ after $n$ steps. It shows that the maximum is governed by binomial coefficients and depends only on the parity of $n$ and $r$.
The result appears in Feller’s classic text (Introduction to Probability Theory, vol. I, 3rd ed., 1968) as a corollary of the ballot‑problem and reflection‑principle techniques.
It is sometimes referred to as the "last‑return" or "last‑zero" theorem and is a cornerstone in the study of random‑walk excursions and bridges.

The "last return" to the origin splits the whole trajectory into a "returning" part and a "non‑returning" part. Because the walk is memoryless and symmetric, the two parts behave like independent random walks of the appropriate lengths.

The factor \(u_{2k}\) measures how likely it is to be at the origin after 2k steps, while \(u_{2m-2k}\) measures the chance that, starting from the origin, the walk avoids the origin for the remaining 2m‑2k steps. Their product therefore captures exactly the event that the final zero occurs at 2k.

A walk whose last return to the origin is at time 2k can be uniquely decomposed into two independent sub‑walks:

1. A walk of length 2k that starts at the origin and ends at the origin. The number of such walks is \(\binom{2k}{k}\), and the probability of each is \(2^{-2k}\), giving probability \(u_{2k}=\binom{2k}{k}/2^{2k}\).

2. A walk of length 2m-2k that starts at the origin and never returns to the origin. The number of such walks is \(\binom{2m-2k}{m-k}\) (the Catalan‑type count for walks staying positive after the first step), and the probability of each is \(2^{-(2m-2k)}\), giving probability \(u_{2m-2k}=\binom{2m-2k}{m-k}/2^{2m-2k}\).

Since the two sub‑walks are independent, the probability of their concatenation is the product \(u_{2k}\,u_{2m-2k}\). Multiplying the numerators and denominators yields the equivalent binomial‑coefficient expression \(\frac{\binom{2k}{k}\binom{2m-2k}{m-k}}{2^{2m}}\).
The special case \(k=0\) corresponds to walks that never return to the origin after time 0, and the formula reduces to \(u_{2m}\), confirming the interpretation.

- k=2 (last return at time 4): probability = u_{4}=3/8 (the walk ends at the origin).
These three probabilities sum to 1, as required.

The formula gives the exact distribution of the time of the final zero of a symmetric random walk of even length. It tells us how likely it is that the walk will stay away from the origin for the last \(m-k\) pairs of steps.

Because the expression is symmetric in k and m-k, the distribution is symmetric around the midpoint \(k=m/2\). This symmetry underlies the result in Exercise 6(b) that, when m is odd, the probability of no equalization in the last m steps is 1/2.
The theorem links two classical combinatorial quantities: the central binomial coefficient (through u_{2k}) and the Catalan‑type count of paths that avoid zero (through u_{2m-2k}).

The result appears as Exercise 7 in the cited text and is a special case of the ballot theorem proved by André and later popularised by Feller (see Feller, *Introduction to Probability Theory*, vol. I, 1968).  It is closely related to the reflection principle and to the enumeration of Dyck paths, which were first studied in the 19th century in the context of Catalan numbers.
Equivalently, the probability of no equalization in the first $2m$ outcomes equals the probability of an equalization exactly at time $2m$, and also equals $P(S_1ge0,dots,S_{2m}ge0)$.

One proof proceeds by decomposing any walk of length $2m$ according to the time $2k$ of its last return to the origin (with $0le kle m$).  The number of walks whose last return occurs at $2k$ is $ inom{2k}{k} inom{2m-2k}{m-k}=2^{2m}u_{2k}u_{2m-2k}$.  Summing over $k$ gives 
$$sum_{k=0}^m inom{2k}{k} inom{2m-2k}{m-k}=2^{2m}u_{2m},,$$ 
so the term $k=0$ (no return at any positive time) contributes $2^{2m}u_{2m}$ walks, i.e. probability $u_{2m}$.  An alternative proof uses the reflection (ballot) principle: the event ${S_1ge0,dots,S_{2m}ge0}$ is in bijection with walks that never hit the origin after time 0, and the ballot theorem gives exactly $ inom{2m}{m}/2^{2m}$.  A third argument notes that the number of such walks equals the Catalan number $C_m= rac1{m+1} inom{2m}{m}$ multiplied by $2$, and dividing by $2^{2m}$ again yields $u_{2m}$.

The theorem says that the chance of staying strictly on one side of the origin for $2m$ steps is the same as the central binomial coefficient divided by $2^{2m}$; this is the classic Catalan‑type result that Dyck paths (paths that never go below the axis) are counted by $ inom{2m}{m}$. Theorem 12.4 is presented in the context of the arc sine laws in section 12.3 of the text, following the analysis of the distribution of the last equalization time in a symmetric random walk (Equation 12.9). It is attributed to results originally found in Feller, specifically on pp. 93–94 of his classic book, where similar relationships between lead times in a game of Heads or Tails and arc sine distributions were first established. For a symmetric random walk the location of the first maximum, when scaled by n, is not uniformly distributed but instead follows an arc‑sine law. The probability that the first maximum occurs before a proportion α of the steps tends to (2/π) arcsin √α, reflecting the fact that extremes tend to occur near the start or the end rather than in the middle.

Let F be a symmetric continuous distribution function, and let α be a fixed real number strictly between 0 and 1. Consider a random walk of length n in which each step has distribution F. Then as n → ∞ we have P(K_n < nα) → (2/π) arcsin √α.

The concept of mean first passage time emerges within the study of ergodic Markov chains, where one analyzes how long the chain typically takes to move from one state to another, or to return to the same state.  The text presents the notion as part of the broader section on descriptive quantities for ergodic chains, indicating its relevance for understanding long‑term behavior.  While the excerpt does not trace its historical origins, it situates the idea alongside the fundamental matrix used in absorbing Markov chains, a standard technique in classical Markov chain theory.

For an ergodic Markov chain that visits every state infinitely often, the mean first passage time captures the expected waiting time until the chain first reaches a given state after leaving it.  Because the chain is recurrent and aperiodic, such a time exists and is finite.  Intuitively, it measures how quickly the chain “mixes” into a particular state, providing a quantitative description of how the stationary distribution’s weights translate into actual travel times between states.

Let •P• be the transition matrix of an ergodic chain with states s_1,•s_2,ldots,•s_r.  For a fixed target state s_j, the mean first passage time •m_{ij}• from state s_i to s_j is defined as the expected number of steps required for the chain to hit state s_j for the first time, given that it starts in state s_i.  The mean time to return to state s_j is the special case where i=j.  These expectations are obtained by treating s_j as an absorbing state (setting p_{jj}=1) and computing the fundamental matrix •N• of the resulting absorbing chain; the •k•th entry of •N• gives the expected number of visits to state k before absorption.  The mean first passage time from i to j is then the (•i•,•j•) entry of this fundamental matrix.
11.5 Mean First Passage Time

In the section, the chain’s long‑run proportion of time in state s_j is w_j, the jth component of the stationary distribution •w•.  This implies that if the chain starts in any state, it will eventually reach s_j infinitely often, and the mean first passage time from any state i to j is finite.  The text further illustrates this by constructing an absorbing chain: set p_{jj}=1 for the target state s_j, keep all other transition probabilities unchanged, and note that the new chain will be absorbed in s_j with probability one.  The fundamental matrix N of this absorbing chain then yields the expected number of visits to each state before absorption, which directly provides the mean first passage times.

••P•: transition matrix of the ergodic chain.
••w = (w_1,ldots,w_r): unique stationary distribution satisfying •w•P = •w•.
••s_j: jth state of the chain.
••p_{jj}=1: modification to make state s_j absorbing for the auxiliary chain.
••N: fundamental matrix of the absorbing chain; its (•i•,•j•) entry equals the expected number of visits to state i before absorption in j.
••m_{ij}: mean first passage time from state i to state j.

The mean first passage time quantifies how long, on average, it takes for the Markov chain to move from one state to another before the first hit.  Because the chain is ergodic, every state can be reached from every other, so these expected times are always finite.  They provide a more detailed understanding of the chain’s dynamics than the stationary probabilities alone, revealing not just the frequency of visits but the temporal spacing between visits.  In particular, larger stationary probabilities correspond, intuitively, to states that are reached more quickly on average, but the actual mean first passage times depend also on the transition structure.

••Finite for all i,j in an ergodic chain (due to recurrence and aperiodicity).
••Symmetry is not guaranteed: •m_{ij}• can differ from •m_{ji}•.
••Related to stationary distribution: the expected return time to state j equals 1/w_j.
••Can be computed via the fundamental matrix N of an auxiliary absorbing chain where p_{jj}=1.
••Mean first passage times satisfy linear equations derived from the transition probabilities, allowing their calculation by solving a system of linear equations.

An absorbing state is a state that, once entered, cannot be left (its self‑transition probability equals 1). An absorbing Markov chain therefore consists of at least one such “sticky’’ state together with other states that eventually “drift’’ into one of the absorbing states. The process is said to be “absorbed’’ when it first reaches an absorbing state, after which it remains there forever.

In an absorbing Markov chain the process eventually enters a state that, once reached, cannot be left. The matrices Q and R describe, respectively, transitions among transient states and transitions from transient to absorbing states, while the fundamental matrix N gives the expected number of visits to each transient state before absorption. Multiplying N by the column vector of ones yields the expected time to absorption (t), and N R yields the absorption probabilities (B).
The process can be visualized as a random walk that eventually gets trapped in an absorbing state, analogous to a game that ends when a player either wins all money or loses everything.

In the gene‑type absorption example the number of genes of a particular type behaves like a fair game; the probability of eventual absorption in a state with that gene type equals the initial proportion of that type.

The gambling interpretation treats each arrival of a gambler as a unit of cash taken by the casino (1 dollar) and the only payouts occur when the target pattern B is completed; because each bet is perfectly fair, the casino’s expected intake must equal its expected payout, leading directly to the expected time to absorption being equal to the total payout BB.

In the random‑walk model on {0,…,N} with absorbing endpoints, the intuition is that once the walk hits 0 or N it stays there forever, so the long‑run behavior is determined entirely by the probability of absorption at each endpoint, which can be computed via harmonic functions.

Definition 11.1: A state $s_i$ of a Markov chain is called absorbing if $p_{ii}=1$, i.e., it is impossible to leave that state. A Markov chain is absorbing if (i) it has at least one absorbing state, and (ii) from every state it is possible to reach an absorbing state (not necessarily in one step).
Definition 11.2: In an absorbing Markov chain, any state that is not absorbing is called transient.

An absorbing Markov chain is a Markov chain whose transition matrix can be written in canonical form \(\displaystyle P=\begin{pmatrix} I & 0\\ R & Q\end{pmatrix}\) where I is the identity matrix on the absorbing states, Q contains the transition probabilities among the transient states, and R contains the transition probabilities from transient to absorbing states. The fundamental matrix is defined as N=(I-Q)^{-1}. The absorption‑probability matrix is B=N R and the vector of expected times to absorption is t=N\mathbf{c} with \mathbf{c} a column vector of ones.

The distribution function assigns probabilities to each possible outcome of a discrete random experiment, allowing us to understand how likely each result is and to compute probabilities of related events. A distribution function can be imagined as a way of distributing a unit of probability mass among all the possible outcomes of an experiment. Each outcome receives a non‑negative weight, and the total of all these weights is exactly one, so that the distribution describes the likelihood of each outcome occurring. This viewpoint makes it clear that a distribution function is simply a probability mass function over a finite or countable sample space.

The function m(ωj) represents the probability that X equals the corresponding outcome ωj. This definition ensures that the total probability over all outcomes equals one, and each individual probability is between 0 and 1.

The Labouchere system is a betting procedure where the player writes a list of numbers, usually 1, 2, 3, 4. The bet placed at each step is the sum of the first and last numbers of the current list. If the bet is won, the first and last numbers are deleted from the list; if the bet is lost, the amount of the last bet is appended to the end of the list. The process is repeated using the updated list, and if the list contains only one number, that number is bet. The game continues until the list becomes empty. At that point the player has won the total sum of the original list. The system is designed so that each win removes two numbers and each loss adds one new number, thereby adjusting the bet size depending on past outcomes.

If any bet loses, the last bet amount is appended to the list, e.g., after losing the first 5‑dollar bet the list becomes 1,2,3,4,5, and the next bet would be 1+5=6.
If the process terminates (the list becomes empty) the player wins the sum of the original numbers, which in this example is 10.

The impossibility of a uniform distribution on a countably infinite sample space is noted in many introductory probability texts (see Definition 1.3), often illustrated by the argument that assigning the same probability a to every outcome ω∈Ω forces either the total mass ∑_ω a to be infinite (if a>0) or zero (if a=0), violating the axiom that the total probability must equal 1.

The uniform distribution function captures the intuitive idea that when no outcome is favored over any other, each outcome should be considered equally likely, reflecting symmetry or fairness in the experiment.
A uniform distribution expresses the intuitive idea that every elementary outcome is equally likely; for a finite set this means each outcome receives the same share of the total probability mass.
Choosing a value uniformly at random from an interval means that every sub‑interval of the same length is equally likely, as illustrated by the probability calculations for r and α.

A uniform distribution function on a finite sample space \(\Omega\) with \(n=|\Omega|\) assigns the same probability \(1/n\) to every elementary outcome \(\omega\in\Omega\); consequently, for any event \(A\subseteq\Omega\) the probability is \(P(A)=|A|/n\).
For a finite sample space Ω with |Ω|=n, a uniform distribution is the probability mass function m defined by m(ω)=1/n for every ω∈Ω, satisfying ∑_{ω∈Ω}m(ω)=1 and m(ω)≥0.

For a countably infinite sample space Ω={ω₁,ω₂,…}, a uniform distribution would require a constant a such that m(ω_i)=a for all i. The axioms of probability demand a≥0 and ∑_{i=1}^{∞}a=1, which is impossible because the series either diverges (if a>0) or equals 0 (if a=0).

If a variable X is chosen uniformly from an interval [a,b], the probability that X lies in a sub‑interval [c,d]⊆[a,b] is (d‑c)/(b‑a), i.e., the length of the sub‑interval divided by the length of the whole interval; similarly, for a point chosen uniformly in a region, the probability equals the area of the sub‑region divided by the total area.

For a six‑sided die each face \(1,2,\dots,6\) has probability \(1/6\); the probability of rolling an even number is \(3/6=1/2\). A fair coin toss has two outcomes each with probability \(1/2\). The text also notes that a uniform distribution cannot be defined on a countably infinite space such as \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,\dots\}\) because assigning the same positive probability to each outcome would make the total sum diverge.

The Monte Carlo procedure is presented as a method for estimating quantities that are difficult or impossible to calculate exactly, using chance experiments; the text also references an earlier chance‑based method for estimating π discovered by G. L. Buffon in 1836, indicating a historical lineage of probabilistic estimation techniques.

The intuition behind a Monte Carlo procedure is that, when points are drawn uniformly at random from a region (e.g., the unit square), the proportion of points that fall into a target subset approximates the subset’s area because probability equals area for a uniform distribution.

A Monte Carlo procedure estimates the measure of a set E (such as an area or a probability) by generating n independent uniformly distributed random points in a known superset (e.g., the unit square) and computing the estimator \(\hat p = \frac{\text{number of points in }E}{n}\); the estimate of the measure of E is then \(\hat p\times \text{measure of the superset}\).

Example 2.2 uses a Monte Carlo procedure to estimate the area under the curve \(y=x^2\) in the unit square by generating random pairs \((x,y)\) and counting the fraction that satisfy \(y\le x^2\); with 10,000 trials the estimate was 0.325, close to the exact value \(1/3\).

The same Monte Carlo idea is applied to estimate π by generating random points in the unit square and counting how many fall inside the inscribed circle of radius ½; the probability of falling inside equals \(\pi/4\), so the estimate of π is \(4\times\)the observed fraction.

The text denotes the target region by \(E\), the random point by \((x,y)\), the estimator by the fraction of points in \(E\), and the probability of the event by \(P(E)\). The Monte Carlo program is referenced simply as **MonteCarlo**.

The fraction of random points landing in \(E\) is interpreted as an empirical probability, which, under a uniform distribution, equals the geometric area of \(E\); thus the Monte Carlo estimate provides an empirical approximation of the true area or probability.

The Monte Carlo estimator converges to the true value as the number of trials \(n\) increases; the expected error decreases at a rate of at most \(1/\sqrt{n}\) with 95 % confidence, as illustrated by the 10,000‑trial example yielding an error around 0.01.

The procedure is applicable to any measurable subset of the unit square (or any space where a uniform distribution can be defined), making it a versatile tool for numerical integration and probability estimation.

Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon (1707-1788) was an eighteenth‑century natural scientist who applied probability to various investigations, publishing his work in the 44‑volume Histoire Naturelle and its supplements.

In his original formulation of the needle problem Buffon described a game where two gamblers drop a loaf of French bread on a wide‑board floor and bet on whether the loaf falls across a crack; he derived the fair‑game condition L = (π/4)W, where L is the length of the loaf (needle) and W the spacing of the cracks (floorboards).
Buffon later considered a checkerboard floor and gave an incorrect answer, which was later corrected by Laplace.

Numerous empirical attempts to estimate π using Buffon's needle are listed in Table 2.1, including experiments by Wolf (1850, π≈3.1596), Smith (1855, π≈3.1553), De Morgan (c.1860, π≈3.137), Fox (1864, π≈3.1595), Lazzerini (1901, π≈3.1415929), and Reina (1925, π≈3.1795).

N. T. Gridgeman (1960) analyzed these experiments, noting that even 10 000 drops could only reliably fix the first decimal of π, and that Lazzerini’s estimate coincided with the Chinese approximation 355/113; Gridgeman inferred Lazzerini’s needle length was 5/6 of the line spacing by applying Buffon's formula with π=355/113.

The needle problem asks: if a thin needle of length L is dropped at random onto a plane ruled with equally spaced parallel lines a distance W apart, what is the chance that the needle crosses one of the lines?

Intuitively, the event of crossing depends on two random quantities: the perpendicular distance d from the needle’s centre to the nearest line (uniform in [0, W/2]) and the acute angle θ between the needle and the lines (uniform in [0, π/2]).
A crossing occurs whenever d ≤ (L/2) sin θ; thus the probability is the proportion of the (d,θ) rectangle that satisfies this geometric inequality.

Let the distance between adjacent parallel lines be W and let the needle length satisfy 0 < L ≤ W. Choose independently a distance d ∈ [0, W/2] uniformly and an angle θ ∈ [0, π/2] uniformly. Define the event E = {d ≤ (L/2) sin θ}. Then the probability of a crossing is P(E) = (2L)/(πW).
If L > W the formula generalises to P(E) = (2/π)(L/W) – (1/π)(L/W)√{(L/W)² – 1} + (2/π)arcsin(W/L).

In Lazzerini’s 1901 experiment a needle of nominal length 0.8333 W was dropped 3 408 times; it crossed a line 1 808 times, giving an empirical crossing probability 1 808/3 408≈0.5303. Inserting L/W=5/6 and π≈355/113 into Buffon’s formula yields P(E)=2·(5/6)/(π)≈0.5303, confirming the consistency of the data.

A simple Monte‑Carlo simulation that generates 100 000 random (d,θ) pairs and counts the fraction satisfying d ≤ (L/2) sin θ reproduces the theoretical probability (2L)/(πW) to within statistical error.
L – length of the needle (or bread loaf).
W – spacing between parallel lines (or width of floorboards).
d – perpendicular distance from the needle’s centre to the nearest line, 0 ≤ d ≤ W/2.
θ – acute angle between the needle and the lines, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2.
E – event that the needle crosses a line.
P(E) – probability of the crossing event.
π – the mathematical constant, appearing in the analytical expression for P(E).
Buffon’s needle provides a geometric method to estimate π: solving P(E)= (2L)/(πW) for π gives π ≈ (2L)/(W·P̂(E)), where P̂(E) is the observed crossing frequency.
The experiment illustrates geometric probability, where probabilities are ratios of areas (or volumes) in a configuration space rather than counts of equally likely outcomes.

Different experimental designs (e.g., varying the way the midpoint is chosen) can lead to different probability assignments, as highlighted by Bertrand’s paradox; the needle problem avoids this ambiguity by using the natural uniform measures on d and θ.
The crossing probability is linear in the needle‑to‑line spacing ratio L/W when L ≤ W, making the estimator for π unbiased: π̂ = (2L)/(W·P̂(E)).
The variance of the estimator decreases as the number of drops N increases, with standard error proportional to 1/√N, so accuracy improves with larger samples.
If the needle length exceeds the line spacing, the probability formula becomes piecewise and involves arcsine terms, reflecting the additional ways a longer needle can intersect a line.
Uniform randomness in both centre position and orientation is essential; any bias in the distribution of d or θ will distort the estimated probability and hence the π estimate.

A density function $f(x)$ describes how probability mass is spread over a continuum of outcomes; the area under $f(x)$ over any interval equals the probability that the random variable falls in that interval, just as the height of a histogram approximates relative frequencies.

In the infinitesimal view, $f(x)dx$ can be thought of as the probability of the outcome falling in an infinitesimally small interval around $x$, even though the probability of any single exact outcome $x$ is zero.

A function $f:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ is called a density function for a continuous random variable $X$ if for every measurable set $E$ we have $P(X\in E)=\int_E f(x)\,dx$, and in particular $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1$.
Equivalently, for any interval $[c,d]$ the probability $P(c\le X<d)=\int_c^d f(x)\,dx$; this relationship is identified as the defining property of density functions in the text.
For the spinner experiment on $[0,1)$ the density function is the constant function $f(x)=1$, yielding $P(c\le X<d)=d-c$ for any $0\le c<d\le1$.

The counting technique described here originates from classical combinatorics and is often presented as the “product rule” for counting the number of outcomes of a multi‑stage experiment, a foundational idea in probability theory.

If a task is performed in successive stages and each stage can be completed in a certain number of ways that does not depend on earlier choices, then the total number of complete tasks is obtained by multiplying the numbers of ways for each stage, reflecting the idea that each choice at one stage can be paired with each choice at the next.

A counting technique (product rule) states that for a task carried out in r sequential stages, where stage i can be performed in n_i distinct ways (independent of previous stages), the total number of possible complete tasks is N = n_1\cdot n_2\cdot\dots\cdot n_r = \prod_{i=1}^{r} n_i.

Example 3.1: At a restaurant you choose an appetizer (2 options), a main course (3 options), and a dessert (2 options). Because the choice at each stage is independent of the others, the total number of distinct three‑course meals is 2\times3\times2 = 12.

Tree‑diagram illustration: If 80% of customers pick soup and then 50% of those pick meat, the joint probability for the path “soup then meat” is (8/10)\times(1/2)=4/10, showing that the product of stage probabilities gives the probability of a complete outcome; the same multiplication principle underlies the counting of the number of such paths.
The total number of outcomes is denoted by N, with individual stage counts denoted n_1,n_2,\dots,n_r. The compact product notation \displaystyle N=\prod_{i=1}^{r} n_i is commonly used.

The technique interprets each possible choice at a given stage as a branch that can be followed by any of the choices at the next stage; the branching structure of a tree diagram visualizes this multiplication, and the final count N represents the size of the sample space of all possible complete paths.

Multiplication is associative and commutative, so the order in which stages are listed does not affect the total count; the technique applies only when the number of options at each stage is independent of earlier selections; it extends naturally to probability calculations by assigning each branch a probability and taking the product to obtain joint probabilities.

The falling factorial notation $(n)_r$ denotes the product $n(n-1)dots(n-r+1)$; it is used in formulas such as $p_r= rac{(365)_r}{365^r}$ for the birthday problem.

A permutation represents a complete reordering of all elements of a set; the requirement of being one‑to‑one and onto ensures that every element appears exactly once in the output ordering.
Counting permutations corresponds to counting the number of distinct ways to arrange $n$ objects, which is given by the factorial $n!$.
